questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 1: The Long Timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean
questions.question_text: How do historians in this book define a civilization?

options.A: A society whose art, music, and moral ideas are more advanced than its neighbors'
options.B: A complex society with cities, a food surplus, specialists, government, records, and monumental buildings
options.C: Any group of people who share one language, one religion, and one ruling family
options.D: A society that has learned to work iron and trade it across the sea

questions.explanation: The chapter uses "civilization" in a narrow, neutral sense: a complex society built around cities, where a food surplus supports specialists, a government organizes large projects, people keep records, and monumental buildings express shared beliefs. It is a checklist, not a ranking, so option A, which treats civilization as a grade of advancement, is exactly the everyday meaning the chapter sets aside. Language, religion, or iron-working alone do not make a civilization.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 1: The Long Timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean
questions.question_text: What is stratigraphy, the most important idea in archaeology?

options.A: Dating a site by counting the coins and inscriptions found on its surface
options.B: Measuring how fast carbon decays in seeds, bones, and charcoal
options.C: Comparing the stories in Homer's poems with the ruins found at a site
options.D: Studying the layers of a site, where deeper layers are older in undisturbed ground

questions.explanation: Stratigraphy is the study of layers. When people live in one place for a long time they build on the rubble of earlier buildings, so each layer holds the remains of one period, and in undisturbed ground the deeper layers are older. Radiocarbon dating (option B) and coins and inscriptions (option A) are tools archaeologists use to date those layers, but they are not stratigraphy itself. Matching ruins to Homer is what led Schliemann astray.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 1: The Long Timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean
questions.question_text: Why do archaeologists consider Heinrich Schliemann's "Priam's Treasure" at Troy a famous error?

options.A: The gold came from Troy II, about a thousand years too early, and his trench damaged the layers closer to Homer's world
options.B: The gold turned out to be a modern forgery that Schliemann had bought from local dealers
options.C: The gold came from Troy IX, a Roman city built long after the Trojan War
options.D: The gold was found at Knossos on Crete and only later moved to Troy

questions.explanation: Schliemann dug a huge trench toward the deepest layers, expecting Homer's Troy there. The hoard he named after King Priam actually came from Troy II, about a thousand years before any plausible date for the Trojan War, and his trench destroyed parts of Troy VI and VII, the layers closer to Homer's world. The chapter never calls the gold a forgery, and Troy IX is the top, latest layer, not the source of the hoard.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 1: The Long Timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean
questions.question_text: A sign at the Acropolis notes an event of 480 BCE. Using the chapter's rule for spans that cross from BCE to CE, how many years separate that event from our trip in 2026 CE?

options.A: 2,506 years
options.B: 1,546 years
options.C: 2,505 years
options.D: 2,507 years

questions.explanation: Because there was no year zero, 1 BCE is followed directly by 1 CE. To measure a span that crosses the line, add the two numbers and subtract one: 480 + 2026 − 1 = 2,505 years. Option A, 2,506, is the common mistake of simply adding the two years. Option B subtracts 480 from 2026, which treats a BCE year as if it were a CE year. The same rule produces the 5,225 years used in the chapter's 24-hour clock.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 1: The Long Timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean
questions.question_text: What is the main lesson of squeezing 5,225 years of history into a single 24-hour clock?

options.A: Most important events in the region happened in the last few hundred years
options.B: Every period on the timeline lasted roughly the same amount of time
options.C: Proportion: the Bronze Age fills the morning, while the Classical period lasts only 43 minutes
options.D: The Byzantine period was too short to leave many buildings on our route

questions.explanation: A timeline's value lies more in proportion than in any single date. On the 24-hour clock the Bronze Age fills the whole morning, the Classical period that most people mean by "ancient Greece" lasts only 43 minutes, and the Byzantine period takes more than five hours of the evening. That directly contradicts option D, and it shows the periods were very unequal in length, which rules out option B.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 1: The Long Timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean
questions.question_text: Which description best fits the Pax Romana?

options.A: About two centuries of unusual internal peace, from Augustus in 27 BCE to the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE
options.B: A peace treaty between Rome and Persia that ended the wars of Alexander's successors
options.C: The years after Constantine founded Constantinople, when the empire became Christian
options.D: A short truce in 67 BCE after Pompey cleared the Mediterranean of pirates

questions.explanation: The Pax Romana, "Roman peace," was a period of about two centuries, from Augustus becoming emperor in 27 BCE to the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE, when most provinces enjoyed internal stability. Pompey's pirate campaign of 67 BCE (option D) was one of its practical foundations, not the peace itself. The chapter also stresses its price: the peace was imposed by force and paid for with heavy provincial taxes.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 1: The Long Timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean
questions.question_text: Paul was a Jew from Tarsus writing to communities ruled by Rome, including Rome itself. Why did he write his letters in Greek?

options.A: Latin was forbidden for religious writing in the first century CE
options.B: He had been trained as a philosopher in Athens, where only Greek was spoken
options.C: Greek was the official language of the Roman government in Rome
options.D: Alexander's conquests had made Koine Greek the shared language of the eastern Mediterranean

questions.explanation: The Hellenistic period answers the puzzle. Three centuries before Paul, Alexander's conquests had spread Greek across the East, and Koine, "common" Greek, became the everyday language of trade and government. Even under Rome the East kept speaking it, and many people in Rome itself spoke it too, so one letter could be read aloud in Ephesus, Corinth, and Rome. Option C misses the point: Greek spread through everyday trade and travel as a lingua franca, the way English does today, not by Roman decree.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 1: The Long Timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean
questions.question_text: What is Anatolia?

options.A: The European part of Turkey around Istanbul, west of the Bosphorus
options.B: The great peninsula forming the Asian part of Turkey, named from the Greek word for "sunrise"
options.C: The chain of islands in the southeastern Aegean that includes Rhodes
options.D: The region around Athens that formed the territory of the ancient city

questions.explanation: Anatolia is the great peninsula that makes up the Asian part of Turkey, about 97 percent of the country. Its name comes from the Greek *anatolē*, "sunrise," because it was the land toward the rising sun, and older books call it Asia Minor. Option C describes the Dodecanese, and option D describes Attica. The chapter stresses that some of the most important Greek cities, such as Troy, Ephesus, and Miletus, were in Anatolia.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 1: The Long Timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean
questions.question_text: In 405 BCE Sparta destroyed the Athenian fleet on the Dardanelles, and in 220 BCE Rhodes went to war over a toll on the Bosphorus. What idea do both stories illustrate?

options.A: Whoever held a narrow chokepoint on the sea lanes could control trade, food, and power
options.B: Large land armies, not navies, decided most wars in the ancient Aegean
options.C: Greek city-states rarely fought each other once Persia had been defeated
options.D: Tolls on shipping made the Bosphorus too costly for traders to use

questions.explanation: Both stories show the power of chokepoints, narrow places where land squeezes the sea. With its fleet gone, Athens could not protect the grain ships coming through the Dardanelles and surrendered. Rhodes, whose wealth came from free trade, fought Byzantium until the Bosphorus tolls were dropped. In both cases the decisive weapon was a strip of water, not an army, which rules out option B. The Rhodian victory also means the tolls did not shut the strait (option D).

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 1: The Long Timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean
questions.question_text: At Ephesus a site guide calls a building from 100 BCE "Roman," while our timeline places the same date in the Hellenistic period. What is the best way to analyze the disagreement?

options.A: The guide is wrong, because the Roman period everywhere begins with the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE
options.B: Our timeline is wrong, because the Hellenistic period ended when Alexander died in 323 BCE
options.C: The building must have been rebuilt by the Romans, so the guide is describing a later layer
options.D: Both are using a valid definition: Rome reached Ephesus before 31 BCE, while our timeline uses one region-wide boundary

questions.explanation: The Roman period is an era label for a place: the years when that place was under Roman rule. Rome arrived at different stops at different times, reaching Ephesus about a century before Rhodes, so a local label can say "Roman" for a date our region-wide timeline still calls Hellenistic. Neither is wrong, which rules out options A and B. The first question is always which definition a label is using; nothing suggests the building was rebuilt.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
questions.question_text: Which list gives the six principles of the thoughtful traveler used throughout this guide?

options.A: Planning, punctuality, packing, budgeting, safety, and photography
options.B: Courtesy, generosity, tolerance, honesty, silence, and gratitude
options.C: Curiosity, humility, consent, reciprocity, patience, and many stories
options.D: Empathy, modesty, thrift, preparation, flexibility, and respect for law

questions.explanation: The chapter names six principles: curiosity (look closer), humility (we are guests), consent (people and sacred places are not scenery), reciprocity (fair exchange with local people), patience (a closed gate is information, not an insult), and many stories (listen to more than one account before judging). The other lists contain sensible travel virtues, but they are not the six the guide applies at every stop, starting with the Hagia Sophia worked example.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
questions.question_text: It is a November evening in a taverna in the Old Town of Rhodes. The menu is short and the service is slow. Which response best puts empathy in travel into practice?

options.A: Ask what is good today, ask about the olive harvest, and thank the waiter in Greek
options.B: Ask to see the full summer menu, since visitors have paid for a complete experience
options.C: Return to the ship for dinner, where the kitchen is fully staffed in every season
options.D: Leave a review warning other travelers that Rhodes restaurants are poorly run in November

questions.explanation: Empathy means seeing the moment from the other person's day. The waiter has worked since April, many coworkers have gone home for the winter, the menu has shrunk to what is fresh, and November is olive-harvest month. From his side, a quiet evening is the reward for a hard summer. The empathetic move is easy: ask what is good today, ask about the harvest, and say *efcharistó*. The other choices tell the story only from inside our own day.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
questions.question_text: Why does the Ancient Mediterranean Treasures voyage jump back and forth across three thousand years of history?

options.A: Viking arranges the ports so that guests see the newest sites first and the oldest last
options.B: Several ports are closed in November, so the ship must skip around the Aegean
options.C: The Bronze Age sites are all on islands, and the ship visits islands only at the end
options.D: The ports follow the order of the sea lanes from Istanbul, not the order of history

questions.explanation: The voyage's order is the order of the sea lanes. Ships sail from Istanbul through the Sea of Marmara and the Dardanelles, south along the Turkish coast, then west to Crete and north to Athens. So we meet Byzantine and Ottoman Istanbul first, the Bronze Age at Troy and Knossos in the middle, and Classical Athens at the end. Option C fails because Troy, a Bronze Age site, is on the mainland near Çanakkale.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
questions.question_text: On the night of Day 7 the ship sails from Kuşadası to Rhodes. What should you do with your watch before bed?

options.A: Set it forward one hour, because Greece is one hour ahead of Turkey in November
options.B: Set it back one hour, because Greece is one hour behind Turkey in November
options.C: Leave it alone, because Turkey and Greece share the same time zone all year
options.D: Set it back two hours, because Greece has just ended its summer time

questions.explanation: Turkey stays on UTC+3 all year, while Greece moves its clocks back at the end of October to UTC+2. In November, Greece is therefore one hour behind Turkey, and the ship changes its clocks overnight between Kuşadası and Rhodes. A phone usually updates itself, but a watch or an alarm set the night before may not. Option D is a common slip: Greece's clock change is one hour, and it happened weeks before the cruise.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
questions.question_text: Why is November called the hinge of the year in the Mediterranean climate?

options.A: It is the month when olive trees are planted for the next season's harvest
options.B: It is the coldest month of the year, when snow closes most mountain roads
options.C: It is the month when the Roman calendar began its new year
options.D: The summer high-pressure belt slides south, so the Atlantic storms and rains return

questions.explanation: The Mediterranean climate has hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters. In summer a belt of high pressure blocks the storms coming in from the Atlantic; in autumn that belt slides south and the storms return. November is when the dry season ends and the wet season begins, which is why Vegetius called the seas "closed" from November 11. November is harvest time for olives, not planting time, and the chapter describes mild days rather than the year's coldest.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
questions.question_text: Which three things does the chapter suggest checking the night before each site visit?

options.A: Today's hours and last entry, the weekly closing day, and any prayer, holiday, or strike closures
options.B: The weather forecast, the ticket price, and the best spot for photographs
options.C: The ship's dinner menu, the excursion bus number, and the local currency rate
options.D: The site's founding date, its period on the timeline, and who ruled it then

questions.explanation: In November, opening hours and closures are the most common reason a well-planned day goes wrong. Greek state sites switch to shorter winter hours from November 1, mosques close to visitors during prayers, and markets keep their own days off. So the night before, check today's hours and last entry, the weekly closing day, and any prayer, holiday, or strike closures. Last entry is often 30 minutes or more before closing, so plan around it. Option D describes Part 1's questions for placing a site in its era.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
questions.question_text: Phoenician, Hebrew, and Arabic are examples of which kind of writing system?

options.A: A syllabary, in which each sign stands for a consonant plus a vowel
options.B: A logographic script, in which most signs stand for whole words
options.C: An abjad, in which each sign stands for a consonant and readers supply most vowels
options.D: An alphabet, in which signs stand for vowels and consonants alike

questions.explanation: Phoenician, Hebrew, and Arabic are abjads of 22 to 28 letters: each sign stands for a consonant, and readers fill in most vowels from their knowledge of the language. A syllabary, like Linear B with about 90 signs, writes whole syllables. Logographic scripts, like Egyptian hieroglyphs and Chinese characters, need hundreds or thousands of signs. A true alphabet, like Greek, writes the vowels too, which is exactly what these three scripts do not do.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
questions.question_text: What made the Greek change to the Phoenician letters, around 800 BCE, so important for learning?

options.A: The Greeks invented an entirely new set of letters that were faster to carve in stone
options.B: By turning spare consonant letters into vowels, the Greeks let a reader sound out words they did not already know
options.C: The Greeks reduced the number of letters from about 90 to 22, so scribes could train faster
options.D: The Greeks added pictures for common words, so readers could recognize them at a glance

questions.explanation: Greek could not be read without vowels, so the Greeks took Phoenician letters for consonant sounds Greek lacked and used them as vowels: *aleph* became *alpha*. The change was small, with no new invention, but a reader no longer needed to know a word already in order to read it. That lowered what a learner must know before starting. Option C confuses the alphabet with Linear B's roughly 90 signs; the Phoenician abjad already had 22 letters.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
questions.question_text: Which sequence describes the pattern that the Learning for All stories follow?

options.A: Learning is locked up, a new technology opens it, someone resists, and the circle widens but never all the way
options.B: A ruler decrees schools, teachers are trained, literacy becomes universal, and the old script is forgotten
options.C: A teacher invents a method, students spread it, governments adopt it, and everyone finally learns
options.D: Learning begins with everyone, a priesthood takes control, a revolution frees it, and it is shared equally

questions.explanation: The chapter gives four steps: learning is locked up in a palace, temple, or guild; a new technology or institution, such as a simpler script, a press, or a library, opens it; someone whose power depended on the old way resists; and the circle widens, but never all the way, because someone is left out the first time. The other options end with universal or equal learning, which the pattern explicitly says never happens in one step.

questions.chapter: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
questions.question_text: Why can a large language model give an answer that sounds confident but is wrong?

options.A: It copies its answers from a single website, which may be out of date
options.B: It is programmed with step-by-step rules that sometimes contain errors
options.C: It deliberately invents details to make its answers more interesting to read
options.D: It predicts which words are likely to come next rather than looking facts up

questions.explanation: A large language model is trained on enormous amounts of text and learns, at its core, to predict which word is likely to come next. Because it predicts likely words rather than looking facts up, it can state a precise-sounding guess, such as a prayer-closing time it cannot know. Option B describes older rule-based programs; machine learning adjusts itself from examples instead. The lesson: use AI to explain and translate, and check anything time-sensitive against an official source.

questions.chapter: Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents
questions.question_text: Which description best fits the Bosphorus Strait?

options.A: A wide bay on the Aegean coast that served as Constantinople's main harbor
options.B: A canal dug by the Ottomans to link the Golden Horn with the Sea of Marmara
options.C: The strait near Troy that connects the Sea of Marmara with the Aegean Sea
options.D: A channel about 31 km long linking the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara, dividing Istanbul between Europe and Asia

questions.explanation: The Bosphorus runs about 31 km from the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara, between about 700 m and 3.7 km wide, and divides Istanbul between Europe and Asia. Together with the Dardanelles, it is the only sea route between the Black Sea and the world's oceans. Option C describes the Dardanelles, the other strait on our route. The Golden Horn is the city's harbor inlet, and the Bosphorus is a natural strait, not a dug canal.

questions.chapter: Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents
questions.question_text: According to the story Herodotus tells, why were the founders of Chalcedon called "blind"?

options.A: They had ignored an oracle from Delphi that told them where to settle
options.B: They passed up the better site across the water, with its harbor, sea defenses, fish, and control of the strait
options.C: They built their city without walls, so it was captured almost at once
options.D: They chose a site on the Asian shore, where the farmland was too poor to feed a city

questions.explanation: A Persian general, hearing that Chalcedon was founded seventeen years before Byzantium, said its founders must have been blind to pass up the far better site across the Bosphorus. Byzantium's strengths were the sea's: a harbor, water on three sides, migrating fish, and a toll on passing ships. Chalcedon actually had the better farmland, so option D reverses the facts. The Delphi oracle version (option A) comes from later Roman writers and is almost certainly an embellishment.

questions.chapter: Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents
questions.question_text: What were the Theodosian Decrees?

options.A: Laws of Theodosius I in 391–392 that banned pagan sacrifice and worship and closed the temples
options.B: Orders of Theodosius II in 413 that set the rules for building and guarding the land walls
options.C: The founding charter of Constantinople issued by Constantine in 330
options.D: A treaty that divided the Roman Empire between the emperor's two sons in 395

questions.explanation: In 391 and 392, Theodosius I issued laws that banned pagan sacrifice, closed the temples of the old gods, and forbade pagan worship even in private homes. Their effects reached sites across our route: the oracle at Delphi fell silent by the end of the 300s. The walls (option B) belong to his grandson Theodosius II, and the 395 split of the empire between his sons was a separate event, not a decree about worship.

questions.chapter: Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents
questions.question_text: Why does the chapter treat the gold solidus as one of the reasons the Byzantine Empire lasted 1,123 years?

options.A: Its gold paid for the Theodosian Walls in a single year
options.B: It was the only coin allowed in the Mediterranean, so rivals had to buy it from Constantinople
options.C: Its weight and purity held for about 700 years, so its trustworthiness helped pay soldiers, buy peace, and attract trade
options.D: It was minted from the treasure Constantine captured from Persia, giving the empire endless reserves

questions.explanation: Constantine introduced the solidus around 309, with about 4.5 grams of nearly pure gold, and emperors kept its weight and purity essentially unchanged for about seven hundred years. A merchant in Venice, Cairo, or Kyiv would accept it without weighing it, much like a medieval US dollar. That trust was a source of power: it let the empire pay soldiers, buy peace, and attract trade. The chapter makes no claim that the solidus was the only legal coin or that it funded the walls.

questions.chapter: Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents
questions.question_text: The Theodosian Walls held Constantinople's land side for about a thousand years. Which analysis best explains both their success and their two failures?

options.A: They were taller than any siege tower, and they fell only when the defenders ran out of food
options.B: Five layers trapped attackers under fire from two levels and bought time; the 1204 crusaders came by the harbor side, and only cannon broke them in 1453
options.C: They were built of stone too hard to dig under, and they failed only after earthquakes weakened them
options.D: They were guarded by a huge permanent army, and they fell when Mehmed bribed the commanders

questions.explanation: An attacker met a moat, an outer terrace, the outer wall, an inner terrace, and a higher inner wall, so anyone who climbed the outer wall stood exposed to defenders shooting from two levels. The walls bought time, and invaders usually ran short of food or were struck by disease. No army broke them by force for a thousand years: the 1204 crusaders entered from the Golden Horn, where sea walls were lower, and Mehmed's cannon breached them in 1453. The 447 earthquake was repaired in under two months.

questions.chapter: Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents
questions.question_text: What lesson for AI and education does the chapter draw from Cardinal Bessarion's gift of Greek manuscripts to Venice?

options.A: Learning is safest when it is kept in one great library behind strong walls
options.B: Scholars should move to whichever city is winning the latest war
options.C: Manuscripts are more reliable than printed books and should be preferred
options.D: Learning that is copied, shared, and spread across many places survives when a single school is lost

questions.explanation: Theodosius II's state-paid school of 425 was protected by walls for a thousand years, but what carried Greek learning through the fall of the city was copies. Bessarion gave about 750 manuscripts to Venice on condition they be open to scholars, and they became the core of the Biblioteca Marciana. The chapter's parallel is resilience: openly licensed educational resources are the modern version of that gift. Option A is the opposite lesson, since a single school behind walls can be lost in one day.

questions.chapter: Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents
questions.question_text: Why did Mehmed II build the fortress of Rumeli Hisarı in 1452, a year before the siege?

options.A: To close the Bosphorus so no ship could bring grain or help to Constantinople from the Black Sea
options.B: To house the giant cannon that would later breach the Theodosian Walls
options.C: To guard the Golden Horn against the Venetian fleet anchored inside it
options.D: To serve as his palace while he governed the new city after the conquest

questions.explanation: Mehmed built Rumeli Hisarı at the narrowest point of the Bosphorus, facing the older Anadolu Hisarı across the water. With cannon on both shores, the Ottomans could stop any ship coming from the Black Sea, the source of much of the city's grain and of any help from the Genoese colonies. Contemporaries called it *Boğazkesen*, "strait-cutter" or "throat-cutter." He had closed the strait before firing a shot at the walls. It stands north of the city, not on the Golden Horn.

questions.chapter: Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents
questions.question_text: Where does the name "Istanbul" come from?

options.A: From the Turkish words for "city of Islam," given by Mehmed II in 1453
options.B: From the Latin name of a Roman fort that stood on the Asian shore
options.C: From medieval Greek *eis tin polin*, "to the City," which Turkish speakers heard as one word
options.D: From the name of Byzas, the legendary founder of the Greek colony

questions.explanation: Greeks in the countryside said *eis tin polin*, "into the city" or "to the City," when going to Constantinople, because there was only one City. Turkish speakers heard the phrase as a single word. The Ottomans used it in everyday speech, while official documents usually said *Kostantiniyye*. Byzas (option D) is the legendary source of "Byzantium," the city's older Greek name. Foreigners switched for good after 1930, when the postal service asked for letters addressed to İstanbul.

questions.chapter: Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents
questions.question_text: Reading a Turkish breakfast table as history, which item belongs to the newest layer, and why?

options.A: The olives, because olive trees reached Anatolia only with the Ottomans
options.B: The yogurt, because Turkic herders brought it west only in the 1900s
options.C: The tomatoes, because they arrived from the Americas just before the Republic
options.D: The tea, because Turkey became a tea-drinking nation only after plantations at Rize in the 1930s and 1940s

questions.explanation: Food as history reads a dish in layers. Olives and olive oil are the oldest layer, cultivated long before Byzantium was founded. Yogurt and kaymak come from Turkic herders who moved into Anatolia after 1071. Tomatoes and peppers came from the Americas after 1492 and were common by the 1800s. Tea is newest of all: the Ottomans drank coffee, and Turkey became a nation of tea drinkers in the 20th century, after plantations were planted at Rize.

questions.chapter: Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents
questions.question_text: You are paying for lunch in Istanbul by card, and the machine asks whether to charge you in US dollars or Turkish lira. What should you do?

options.A: Choose Turkish lira, because the dollar conversion offered usually has a worse exchange rate than your own bank
options.B: Choose US dollars, because the lira's inflation makes lira prices unreliable
options.C: Choose US dollars, because Turkish restaurants prefer foreign currency
options.D: Cancel and pay with dollar bills, since cash in dollars is accepted everywhere

questions.explanation: Card machines and ATMs often offer to charge in dollars "for convenience," a service called dynamic currency conversion, and its exchange rate is usually worse than our own bank's. Whenever a screen asks, choose Turkish lira. The lira's inflation (option B) is a reason to check the exchange rate and avoid trusting printed prices, not a reason to pay in dollars. The chapter's rule is to pay in lira, withdrawn from a bank ATM, and to carry small notes for tips.

questions.chapter: Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia
questions.question_text: Procopius praised Justinian in *Buildings* and called him a demon in *The Secret History*, written in the same years. What lesson about primary sources does this teach?

options.A: Ask who wrote a source, for whom, and why, because each book served a different purpose
options.B: A primary source is always more trustworthy than a modern history book
options.C: Procopius was a liar, so neither book can be used as evidence
options.D: The later of two conflicting sources should always be believed

questions.explanation: A primary source comes from the time it describes, but that does not make it true. *Buildings* was written for the emperor and *The Secret History* against him, so the first question is "who wrote this, for whom, and why?" The chapter says plainly that the lesson is not that Procopius was a liar (option C); we need both books, read with their purposes in mind. Option B confuses being close to events with being reliable.

questions.chapter: Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia
questions.question_text: Your guide in Hagia Sophia says Justinian entered the finished church and declared, "Solomon, I have outdone thee." How should you test the story?

options.A: Check whether the line appears on an inscription inside the building today
options.B: Accept it, since guides at major sites repeat only verified quotations
options.C: Find the earliest source and the gap since the event; here it is a text written about three hundred years later
options.D: Compare it with what Mehmed II said when he entered the church in 1453

questions.explanation: The myth-versus-history test is to find the earliest source and ask how long after the event it was written. Procopius in the 550s and Paul the Silentiary in 563 never mention the line. It first appears in the anonymous *Diēgēsis*, around the 8th or 9th century, which also features an angel and a dream. So the line belongs to the myth of Hagia Sophia. It still tells us something real: later residents believed their church had surpassed Solomon's Temple.

questions.chapter: Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia
questions.question_text: Walking through the Basilica Cistern, you notice that the columns and capitals come in many different styles and heights. Which kind of city layer are you seeing?

options.A: Converted: a building that kept its walls but changed its use
options.B: Reused: spolia, stone pieces carried from older buildings into a new one
options.C: Built over: a new structure raised on the rubble of an older one
options.D: Removed: gaps left where looters took away the original columns

questions.explanation: The chapter names four ways a layer is added: built over, reused, converted, and removed. Mismatched columns and capitals are the classic clue for reuse. Such reused pieces are called spolia, Latin for "spoils," and builders used them to save quarrying labor and for prestige. The chapter calls the Cistern "a museum of spolia." Conversion would show additions for a new use, such as minarets on a church, and removal would leave empty niches or bare stone.

questions.chapter: Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia
questions.question_text: What is the difference between restoration and reconstruction?

options.A: Restoration is done by governments, while reconstruction is done by private owners
options.B: Restoration rebuilds missing parts from a best guess, while reconstruction only cleans surfaces
options.C: Restoration applies to mosaics and paintings, while reconstruction applies only to domes
options.D: Restoration repairs and conserves what survives, while reconstruction rebuilds what is lost

questions.explanation: Restoration repairs and conserves the surviving material so it lasts, without inventing what is lost. Reconstruction rebuilds missing parts, from evidence or a best guess. The line matters because a reconstruction can look as old as the original and quietly turn a guess into a fact. Option B reverses the two terms. Hagia Sophia has had both: the dome rebuilt higher after 558 was a reconstruction, while the Fossati brothers' work of 1847–1849 was a restoration.

questions.chapter: Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia
questions.question_text: How are the Nika Riots of 532 connected to the Hagia Sophia we visit today?

options.A: The rioters attacked the newly finished Hagia Sophia because Justinian had taxed them to build it
options.B: Justinian built Hagia Sophia as a fortress where he could hide from future riots
options.C: The fires burned the earlier church of Hagia Sophia, and Justinian began the new one five weeks later
options.D: The riots began inside Hagia Sophia when the Blues and Greens fought over seats

questions.explanation: In January 532, the Blues and the Greens, normally rival racing fans, united in the Hippodrome against Justinian's tax officials. Fires destroyed much of the city center, including the second church of Hagia Sophia. After Theodora persuaded Justinian not to flee, his generals trapped the crowd in the Hippodrome. On February 23, 532, construction of the new Hagia Sophia began on the ashes of the old one. The riots began in the Hippodrome, not the church, and the new building came after them.

questions.chapter: Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia
questions.question_text: Hagia Sophia's first dome partly collapsed in 558, yet the rebuilt dome has stood for about fifteen centuries. Which analysis best explains its survival?

options.A: It was rebuilt 6 to 7 m higher with a steeper curve that pushed outward less, and later builders kept adding buttresses
options.B: It was rebuilt in lightweight concrete, which earthquakes cannot crack
options.C: Its 40 windows were bricked up, which made the dome solid enough to resist earthquakes
options.D: Its two half-domes were removed, so the central dome carries less weight

questions.explanation: After earthquakes in 553 and 557, the eastern part of the shallow first dome fell in 558. Isidore the Younger rebuilt it about 6 to 7 m higher, so its steeper curve pushed outward less. Later partial collapses were repaired, and Byzantine and Ottoman builders, including Sinan in the 1570s, added buttresses to hold the walls in against the dome's thrust. The 40 windows and the two half-domes are still part of the building, which rules out options C and D.

questions.chapter: Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia
questions.question_text: In the Basilica Cistern, a guide says the two Medusa heads were set sideways and upside down to cancel the Gorgon's deadly gaze. Applying the chapter's method, what is the better explanation?

options.A: They were turned over by an earthquake after the Cistern was built
options.B: The builders needed blocks of the right height for two short columns, and those positions fit
options.C: Ottoman engineers flipped them in the 1500s to show the end of pagan beliefs
options.D: They were carved that way on purpose for a Roman temple of Medusa

questions.explanation: No source from 532 explains the placement, so the "cancel her gaze" story fails the myth-versus-history test. The practical explanation fits the evidence: the builders needed blocks of the right height to bring two short columns up to the roof, and sideways and upside down were the positions that fit. That matches the rest of the Cistern, where spolia were used wherever they would fit. Nobody knows which earlier building the heads came from, so option D has no support.

questions.chapter: Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia
questions.question_text: What was Byzantine iconoclasm?

options.A: The split between the churches of Rome and Constantinople in 1054
options.B: The practice of writing icons on wooden panels in strict traditional poses
options.C: The Ottoman covering of Christian mosaics after 1453
options.D: A policy, from about 726 to 843, of banning and destroying religious images as idolatry

questions.explanation: Iconoclasm, Greek for "image-breaking," was the Byzantine policy of banning religious images, in two periods from about 726 to 787 and from 815 to 843, on the belief that venerating them was idolatry. Icons were restored for good in 843 by the regent Theodora, a victory Orthodox churches still celebrate as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. Option A describes the Great Schism, and option B describes how icons are made, not the movement against them.

questions.chapter: Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia
questions.question_text: The Fourth Crusade was called to attack Muslim Egypt but ended by sacking Christian Constantinople in 1204. Which chain of causes best explains the change?

options.A: In debt to Venice, the crusaders took Zara, backed Alexios for the throne, and attacked when his promised money never came
options.B: The pope ordered the crusaders to punish Constantinople for its part in the Great Schism of 1054
options.C: Storms drove the Venetian fleet into the Bosphorus, and the starving crusaders attacked the city for supplies
options.D: The Byzantine emperor invited the crusaders inside the walls, then tried to hold them as hostages

questions.explanation: The crusade went wrong because of money. Fewer crusaders arrived than the 33,500 Venice had built ships for, so they could not pay. Doge Enrico Dandolo let the debt wait if they helped take Zara. Then Alexios Angelos promised 200,000 marks to restore his father. Alexios IV could not pay, was overthrown, and the new emperor refused, so the crusaders and Venetians stormed the sea walls on April 12, 1204. Pope Innocent III had excommunicated them over Zara, so option B is wrong.

questions.chapter: Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia
questions.question_text: What modern parallel does the chapter draw from the Byzantine switch from uncial to minuscule script?

options.A: Handwriting is slower than typing, so students should not learn to write by hand
options.B: New scripts always make old books easier to find and read
options.C: What is not copied into a new medium is left behind, just as AI tutors learn mainly from text digitized in a few languages
options.D: Only professional scribes should decide which books a school reads

questions.explanation: When scribes switched to minuscule in the 9th century, every book had to be copied again. Copying was slow and parchment costly, so works on school reading lists survived and hundreds of others were lost; only 7 of Aeschylus's roughly 90 plays survive. Today's bottleneck is data: AI tutors learn from digitized text, mostly in a handful of languages. The lesson is that deciding what gets copied decides who gets to learn, so the choice should be made widely and on purpose, the opposite of option D.

questions.chapter: Day 3: Ottoman Istanbul, Topkapı, and Friday Prayer
questions.question_text: What does the sequence of gates and courts at Topkapı Palace show about how the palace worked?

options.A: Each court was built by a different sultan, so the gates mark the order of construction
options.B: The gates were defensive, built to stop attackers who had already breached the city walls
options.C: Each gate filtered who could pass, so the courts grew more private from the public First Court to the sultan's Third Court
options.D: The courts separated the palace by religion, with Christians and Muslims housed in different courts

questions.explanation: Topkapı is a sequence of courtyards, each more private than the last. The First Court, through the Imperial Gate, was open to the public. Beyond the Gate of Salutation, only officials on business could enter the Second Court, where the Imperial Council met. The Gate of Felicity led to the Third Court, the sultan's private world. The gates filtered access; the chapter does not describe them as military defenses, construction phases, or religious divisions.

questions.chapter: Day 3: Ottoman Istanbul, Topkapı, and Friday Prayer
questions.question_text: How did the Ottoman sultans come to claim the caliphate, the leadership of the whole Muslim community?

options.A: Mehmed II claimed it when he took Constantinople in 1453
options.B: Suleiman the Magnificent was elected caliph by the scholars of Mecca
options.C: Osman received it from the last Byzantine emperor around 1299
options.D: Selim I took over the claim when he conquered Egypt in 1517

questions.explanation: When Selim I conquered Egypt in 1517, the Ottomans took over the claim to the caliphate, along with the Prophet's relics and the protection of the holy cities, and later sultans used the title to speak for Muslims far beyond their borders. The Turkish Republic abolished the caliphate on March 3, 1924. Mehmed II's conquest of 1453 (option A) brought Ottoman titles such as "Caesar of Rome," not the caliphate.

questions.chapter: Day 3: Ottoman Istanbul, Topkapı, and Friday Prayer
questions.question_text: How does the chapter correct the Western painters' image of the Harem of Topkapı?

options.A: It shows the Harem was a small set of guest rooms rarely used by the sultan's family
options.B: It describes the Harem as a household, a training school, and a center of politics, led by the sultan's mother
options.C: It explains that the Harem was a religious school where women studied the Quran
options.D: It shows the Harem was a prison for princes and had nothing to do with the sultan's family

questions.explanation: Western painters imagined the Harem as a place of idle pleasure, an image that says more about European fantasies than about the Ottomans. In reality the Harem, a maze of more than 300 rooms, was a household, a training school, and a political center. Its most powerful figure was the valide sultan, the sultan's mother, and during the "Sultanate of Women," figures such as Hürrem and Kösem shaped policy and succession. It housed the whole family, not just guests or princes.

questions.chapter: Day 3: Ottoman Istanbul, Topkapı, and Friday Prayer
questions.question_text: It is Friday, November 13, and you hope to see the inside of the Süleymaniye Mosque. When should you plan to visit?

options.A: Spend midday in a museum, bazaar, or café, and visit the mosque later, after the Friday prayer ends
options.B: Arrive just before noon, when the doors open wide for the sermon
options.C: Wait outside the main door during the Friday prayer so you are first in line
options.D: Visit at sunset, since mosques close to visitors only on Friday mornings

questions.explanation: Friday prayer, held at midday in place of the ordinary noon prayer, includes a sermon and fills the big mosques well before noon, with worshippers praying in the courtyard and street. It is the longest closure to visitors of the week. The chapter advises being in a museum, bazaar, or café at midday rather than outside a mosque door, then visiting between prayers. Sunset (option D) is itself a prayer time, so it is a poor choice too.

questions.chapter: Day 3: Ottoman Istanbul, Topkapı, and Friday Prayer
questions.question_text: Inside the Blue Mosque, a man is praying on the carpet between you and the tiles you want to see up close. What does mosque etiquette ask of you?

options.A: Walk quickly in front of him, since visitors are allowed anywhere outside prayer times
options.B: Take a quiet photograph of him praying, as long as the flash is off
options.C: Ask him to move aside so other visitors can reach the tiles
options.D: Stay in the visitors' area and never walk directly in front of someone who is praying

questions.explanation: Mosque etiquette asks visitors to come outside prayer times, dress modestly, take off their shoes before stepping on the carpet, use the visitors' entrance, stay in the visitors' area, and never walk directly in front of someone praying. Photography etiquette adds that we never photograph people at prayer, flash or no flash, which rules out option B. Interrupting a worshipper (option C) would put our visit ahead of his worship, the opposite of being a good guest.

questions.chapter: Day 3: Ottoman Istanbul, Topkapı, and Friday Prayer
questions.question_text: In Hagia Sophia, the mihrab stands in the old Christian apse but is turned a few degrees off-center. What does that angle reveal?

options.A: The building settled unevenly after the earthquake of 558
options.B: Ottoman builders placed it to line up with the Blue Mosque across the park
options.C: Justinian's altar faced east, while prayer faces Mecca to the south-southeast, so the conversion left a readable layer
options.D: The mihrab was moved during the museum years and put back slightly wrong in 2020

questions.explanation: The mihrab is a niche in the qibla wall marking the direction of Mecca. In Hagia Sophia it sits in Justinian's apse but is turned slightly to the south, because a church's altar faces east while Muslim prayer faces Mecca, south-southeast of Istanbul. That small angle is a layer we can read without a guide: the evidence of a church converted into a mosque. Nothing in the chapter links it to earthquakes or to the Blue Mosque.

questions.chapter: Day 3: Ottoman Istanbul, Topkapı, and Friday Prayer
questions.question_text: Which building did Mimar Sinan call his masterpiece?

options.A: The Selimiye Mosque in Edirne
options.B: The Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul
options.C: The Şehzade Mosque in Istanbul
options.D: The Sultan Ahmed (Blue) Mosque in Istanbul

questions.explanation: Sinan described his career in three buildings. The Şehzade Mosque (1543–1548) was his apprentice work, the Süleymaniye (1550–1557) his journeyman work, and the Selimiye in Edirne (1568–1575) his masterpiece, with a single dome about 31 m across, as wide as Hagia Sophia's, on eight slim piers. The Blue Mosque (1609–1616) was built after Sinan's death by Sedefkâr Mehmed Ağa, who had trained under him.

questions.chapter: Day 3: Ottoman Istanbul, Topkapı, and Friday Prayer
questions.question_text: The Süleymaniye's dome is narrower than Hagia Sophia's but almost as high. How does that design reflect what a mosque needs?

options.A: A narrow dome forced worshippers into a long line toward the altar, like a church
options.B: A steeper dome pushes outward less, and with piers built into the walls it creates one wide hall where long rows can face Mecca
options.C: Sinan lacked the skill to build a dome as wide as Hagia Sophia's at any point in his career
options.D: A higher dome was needed so that the call to prayer could be given from inside it

questions.explanation: A church leads the eye along a long axis to the altar; a mosque needs a wide, unified hall where long rows of worshippers stand side by side facing Mecca. The Süleymaniye's dome, about 26.5 m across and 53 m high, is proportionally steeper and pushes outward less. Its piers are partly built into the side walls, so we see one great room. Option C is wrong: Sinan matched Hagia Sophia's width later at Edirne. Option A describes a church plan.

questions.chapter: Day 3: Ottoman Istanbul, Topkapı, and Friday Prayer
questions.question_text: Walking around the Süleymaniye, you see medreses, a hospital, a soup kitchen, a bath, and rows of shops. Which feature of the vakıf explains how the teachers and cooks were paid for centuries?

options.A: The sultan's treasury paid the staff each year from taxes approved by the council
options.B: Students paid tuition, and the fees were shared among the staff
options.C: Property such as the shops was dedicated forever, could never be sold, and its rents paid the staff named in the deed
options.D: Worshippers left coins at the mihrab each Friday to cover the week's wages

questions.explanation: A vakıf permanently dedicates property, such as shops, farmland, or baths, so its income pays forever for a stated purpose. Once dedicated, it can never be sold or inherited. The deed, the vakfiye, lists every staff position and its pay, and a trustee manages the property. There was no ministry of education or health, so option A is wrong, and the schools were free, with stipends for students, so option B is wrong. Some vakıfs ran for four hundred years.

questions.chapter: Day 3: Ottoman Istanbul, Topkapı, and Friday Prayer
questions.question_text: What lesson for AI in education does the chapter draw from the vakıf?

options.A: Free learning should be run directly by the government's budget, not by charities
options.B: Educational technology should charge fees so that it can pay its own way
options.C: A school's curriculum should be fixed forever by its founder so that it cannot be corrupted
options.D: Free learning needs a lasting source of income independent of any one ruler, plus a way to keep changing what it teaches

questions.explanation: Much educational technology is paid for by grants or investors and disappears when the money stops. The vakıf solved that with a permanent engine of income separated from the whims of any one ruler, providing endowed free education. But the same deeds made the schools hard to change, so the curriculum stayed fixed while the world moved on to print. An AI tutor would need lasting income and what the vakıf lacked, a way to keep changing. Option C repeats the vakıf's weakness.

questions.chapter: Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses
questions.question_text: You find a brass lamp you like in the Grand Bazaar. Which approach to bargaining follows the chapter's advice?

options.A: Offer a very low price you would never actually pay, to leave room for the seller to come down
options.B: Decide privately the most you would happily pay before asking the price, then walk toward that number in a friendly way
options.C: Refuse any tea the seller offers, since accepting it obliges you to buy
options.D: Bargain hard over every item in the shop, including the spices sold by weight

questions.explanation: The chapter's shortcut is to set your price before you ask theirs: decide the most you would happily pay and keep it to yourself, so the conversation is a friendly walk toward your number. The rules also say never name a price you would not pay (option A) and do not bargain on food, spices sold by weight, or price-tagged goods (option D). Accepting tea creates no obligation, and walking away politely is always allowed.

questions.chapter: Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses
questions.question_text: Why was pepper that was cheap on India's Malabar Coast so expensive in Venice around 1450, and what changed in 1498?

options.A: Every merchant and ruler along the route took a share, until Vasco da Gama's sea route around Africa skipped the middlemen
options.B: Pepper spoiled quickly on the journey, until the Portuguese learned to dry it in 1498
options.C: Venice taxed spices heavily to fund its fleet, until the Ottomans conquered Venice in 1498
options.D: Pepper grew only in tiny amounts, until new farms in Egypt began producing it in 1498

questions.explanation: A sack of pepper passed from Calicut to Aden, up the Red Sea, across to the Nile, through Cairo to Alexandria, where the Mamluk sultan taxed it and a Venetian bought it. At least five sets of merchants and three sets of rulers took a share. In 1498 Vasco da Gama reached Calicut by sailing around Africa, opening a route that skipped every middleman between India and Lisbon. Spices were valued partly because they did not spoil, which rules out option B.

questions.chapter: Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses
questions.question_text: At the Spice Bazaar, a stall offers a large, cheap bag labeled "Turkish saffron." What is the most likely truth, and what should real saffron look like?

options.A: It is genuine saffron, because Turkey grows so much that it is sold in bulk
options.B: It is saffron from Kozani in Greece, relabeled for tourists
options.C: It is real saffron powder, which is cheaper than threads but has the same flavor
options.D: It is probably safflower; real saffron comes by the gram in small sealed packets of deep red threads

questions.explanation: Big, cheap bags labeled "Turkish saffron" usually hold safflower petals, a different plant that colors food but has none of saffron's flavor. Saffron is the hand-picked stigmas of a crocus, only three per flower, so a kilogram takes around 150,000 flowers. Real saffron is sold by the gram in small sealed packets, its threads deep red with lighter tips and shaped like tiny trumpets. In warm water it releases its color slowly. If the price seems too good, ask to see the threads.

questions.chapter: Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses
questions.question_text: In what order did a Roman bather move through the main rooms of the public baths?

options.A: Hot room, steam room, cold plunge, and then a massage on the navel stone
options.B: Exercise court, library, hot room, and then a warm pool
options.C: Changing room, cold room (*frigidarium*), warm room (*tepidarium*), and hot room (*caldarium*)
options.D: Warm room, hot room, changing room, and then a cold room in the garden

questions.explanation: In Roman bath culture, bathers moved from a changing room to a cold room, the *frigidarium*, then a warm room, the *tepidarium*, then a hot room, the *caldarium*. The rooms were heated by hot air from furnaces circulating under raised floors and inside walls, a system called the hypocaust. The navel stone and the scrub in option A belong to the later Turkish bath, which adapted the Roman custom with steam.

questions.chapter: Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses
questions.question_text: Under the Ottoman millet system, how were non-Muslim communities governed?

options.A: Each religious community, led by its own head, ran its own worship, schools, charities, and family courts, while paying a special tax
options.B: Non-Muslims were required to convert within a generation or leave the empire
options.C: All communities were governed by the same Islamic courts and had identical rights and duties
options.D: Each community elected representatives to a parliament that made laws for the whole empire

questions.explanation: The millet system organized non-Muslims into religious communities, the Greek Orthodox, Armenians, and Jews, each under its own religious head. Each ran its own worship, schools, charities, and courts for marriage, divorce, and inheritance. In return non-Muslims paid the *cizye* poll tax and lived under restrictions, such as needing permission to build churches. So it allowed real self-rule with real limits on equality, which rules out option C. Forced conversion (option B) was the Spanish policy of 1492, not the Ottoman one.

questions.chapter: Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses
questions.question_text: Who were the Sephardic Jewish refugees who settled in the Ottoman Empire after 1492?

options.A: Jews from Germany who fled persecution and spoke Yiddish
options.B: Jews expelled from Spain, welcomed by Sultan Bayezid II, who kept their Judeo-Spanish language, Ladino
options.C: Jews from Jerusalem who came to Istanbul after Mehmed II's conquest and spoke Hebrew
options.D: Jews from Venice who moved to Rhodes with the Knights Hospitaller and spoke Italian

questions.explanation: "Sephardic" comes from *Sefarad*, the Hebrew name for Spain. On March 31, 1492, Ferdinand and Isabella ordered Spain's Jews to convert or leave. Many refugees found a welcome from Sultan Bayezid II and settled in Istanbul, Edirne, İzmir, and above all Salonica. They brought skills in medicine, finance, textiles, and printing, and kept Ladino, a form of 15th-century Spanish. Later, after Suleiman took Rhodes in 1522, Sephardic families settled in its walled town.

questions.chapter: Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses
questions.question_text: On your first morning in Rhodes, your phone shows a different time from the ship's daily program, and the all-aboard time is this afternoon. Which time should you use?

options.A: Your phone's time, because phones always update to the local network automatically
options.B: Turkish time, because the ship is registered to its departure port of Istanbul
options.C: The average of the two times, to leave a safe margin
options.D: Ship's time as announced in the daily program, since the ship will not wait for late passengers

questions.explanation: The all-aboard time is the one number to remember every port day, because the ship will not wait for late passengers on independent outings. When the ship sails from Kuşadası to Rhodes, its clocks go back one hour for Greece. Phones usually update when they find a Greek network, but at sea they may not, and they sometimes pick up a Turkish tower near the coast, which is why option A is risky. The rule is always to use ship's time.

questions.chapter: Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses
questions.question_text: The chapter says a scribe's cost is almost all marginal cost, while a press has a large fixed cost. What does that comparison show?

options.A: Scribes were always cheaper than presses, which is why handwriting lasted so long
options.B: The press was cheaper for single copies but too expensive for large editions
options.C: For one copy the scribe is cheaper, but for many copies the press wins, the same shape as an AI tutor today
options.D: Fixed and marginal costs were equal, so the choice between scribe and press was a matter of taste

questions.explanation: Each new copy by a scribe takes as long as the last, so the cost per copy stays high. A press needs a large up-front cost, casting type, building the press, and setting every page, but each extra copy costs very little. So for one copy the scribe is cheaper, while for a hundred the press wins overwhelmingly. The chapter notes that digital learning has the same shape: a good AI tutor is expensive to build and nearly free to share. Option B reverses the logic.

questions.chapter: Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses
questions.question_text: About 275 years passed between Gutenberg's press and the first Ottoman book printed in Arabic script in 1729. Which analysis best fits the chapter's evidence?

options.A: A 1485 decree by Bayezid II banning printing on pain of death fully explains the delay
options.B: Several causes worked together: reverence for handwritten sacred text, a script needing hundreds of letter forms, scribes' livelihoods, and weak demand
options.C: The Ottomans had never heard of printing until Müteferrika brought the idea from Europe
options.D: Arabic script was physically impossible to print until new technology appeared in the 1720s

questions.explanation: Most historians now think several causes worked together. Handwriting the Quran was an act of devotion; joined letters that change shape need hundreds of sorts; copyists and calligraphers lived by handwriting; and manuscripts met the needs of a small reading public. The famous 1485 ban (option A) survives in no copy, and many historians doubt it existed. The Ottomans knew of printing: Istanbul had a Hebrew press from 1493, which rules out option C, and European printers had already printed Arabic, crudely.

questions.chapter: Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses
questions.question_text: Müteferrika's printed books sat unsold. What lesson does the chapter draw from this for AI tutors?

options.A: Cheap copies do not create readers; an AI tutor reaches only children with a device, a connection, a language it speaks well, and a reason to trust it
options.B: Printing was a failed technology, so AI tutors will probably fail in the same way
options.C: Books should be given away free, because price was the only barrier to reading
options.D: An AI tutor should be built only after every child can already read well

questions.explanation: Printing made copies cheap but did not make readers: by one estimate, only about one person in ten could read Ottoman script on the eve of the 1928 reform. The circle widened for real only when schooling and a simpler script came together. Likewise, an AI tutor has a high cost to build and almost no cost per learner, but it will reach only children who have a device, a connection, a language it speaks well, and a reason to trust it. Price was never the only gate (option C).

questions.chapter: Day 5: The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey
questions.question_text: Why do many historians now prefer "transformation under pressure" to "Ottoman decline"?

options.A: The empire lost very little territory between the siege of Vienna in 1683 and 1922
options.B: The empire was never defeated in war by Austria or Russia
options.C: The phrase "sick man of Europe" was invented by Turkish historians in the 20th century
options.D: A state that lasted 240 years after Vienna, reformed its army, law, and schools, and held at Gallipoli was not simply dying

questions.explanation: The losses were real: Hungary in 1699, Crimea in 1783, and province after province to nationalism and debt. But an empire that kept going for 240 years after Vienna, reformed its army, law, and schools, and fought the Great Powers to a standstill at Gallipoli was not simply dying, so "transformation under pressure" fits better. Options A and B contradict the military defeats the chapter lists. The "sick man" phrase is attributed to the Russian tsar Nicholas I in 1853.

questions.chapter: Day 5: The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey
questions.question_text: On Day 8 in Rhodes you meet an older resident whose grandparents went to Italian schools, while on Day 9 a Cretan mentions great-grandparents who grew up under the sultan. What explains the difference?

options.A: Greek stops joined the modern Greek state at different times: Crete in 1913 and Rhodes only in 1947, after Italian rule
options.B: Rhodes was never part of the Ottoman Empire, while Crete was Ottoman until 1947
options.C: Both islands joined Greece in 1832, but Italy ran Rhodes's schools by treaty
options.D: Crete joined Greece in 1947, while Rhodes joined in 1913 after a short Italian visit

questions.explanation: The modern Greek state grew over 115 years. Athens and Delphi lay inside the first kingdom of 1832. Heraklion became Greek in 1913, so Cretans may have great-grandparents who grew up under the sultan or in the autonomous Cretan State. Rhodes became Greek only in 1947, after 35 years of Italian rule, so its older residents may have grandparents with Italian schooling. Rhodes was Ottoman from 1522, which rules out option B, and option D reverses the dates.

questions.chapter: Day 5: The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey
questions.question_text: How did Mustafa Kemal first become a name the Ottoman public knew?

options.A: As governor of Salonica, where he was born, during the Balkan Wars
options.B: As the officer who negotiated the Treaty of Sèvres in 1920
options.C: As commander of the 19th Division at Gallipoli in 1915, where he stopped the Anzac advance on the heights
options.D: As the leader of the Greek army's defeat at the Battle of Navarino in 1827

questions.explanation: On April 25, 1915, Mustafa Kemal commanded the 19th Division at Gallipoli. When the Anzacs came ashore below the heights, he led his men onto the ridge in time to stop their advance, at great cost, and he held the line again in August. Gallipoli made him a colonel and a public hero. The sultan's government signed Sèvres, which his Ankara Assembly rejected, and Navarino came decades before his birth in 1881.

questions.chapter: Day 5: The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey
questions.question_text: Under the 1923 population exchange, a Turkish-speaking Orthodox Christian family lived in Cappadocia. What happened to them, and why?

options.A: They stayed in Turkey, because they spoke Turkish
options.B: They were sent to Greece, because the exchange sorted people by religion, not language
options.C: They could choose either country, because the exchange was voluntary
options.D: They moved to Istanbul, because all Orthodox Christians were exempted there

questions.explanation: The Lausanne convention of January 1923 required the compulsory exchange of Greek Orthodox Christians in Turkey for Muslims in Greece, and none could return. Its rule was religion, not language: Turkish-speaking Orthodox Christians from Cappadocia went to Greece, and Greek-speaking Muslims from Crete went to Turkey. The exchange was compulsory, not voluntary. The Istanbul exemption covered only Greek Orthodox who had settled there before October 30, 1918, not anyone who moved there.

questions.chapter: Day 5: The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey
questions.question_text: The Treaty of Sèvres took away the Arab provinces and gave Eastern Thrace to Greece. Using the National Pact, what should you predict the Treaty of Lausanne did with these two terms?

options.A: It reversed the Thrace term, which lay inside the Pact's claim, and kept the Arab term, which the Pact had left out
options.B: It kept both terms, because Lausanne simply confirmed Sèvres
options.C: It reversed both terms, returning the Arab provinces and Eastern Thrace to Turkey
options.D: It kept the Thrace term and reversed the Arab term, because Greece had won the war

questions.explanation: The National Pact of 1920 claimed lands with an Ottoman Muslim majority still held by Ottoman forces at the 1918 armistice, and left the Arab provinces to their inhabitants. Eastern Thrace was inside the Pact, and the nationalists won the war, so Lausanne reversed that term and drew the border on the Maritsa River. The Arab provinces were outside the Pact, so Lausanne kept that term. One question, "was it inside the Pact?", predicts most of the treaty. Turkey, not Greece, won.

questions.chapter: Day 5: The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey
questions.question_text: How does secularism in Turkey (*laiklik*) differ from the separation of church and state in the United States?

options.A: Turkey bans all public religious practice, including the call to prayer
options.B: Turkey's constitution makes Sunni Islam the official religion of the state
options.C: Turkey leaves religion entirely to private communities, with no government role
options.D: The Turkish state manages religion, running the mosques and employing their imams through the Diyanet

questions.explanation: *Laiklik*, written into the constitution in 1937, means the state and its law are not based on religion. But rather than staying out of religion, as in the United States, the Turkish state manages it: the Presidency of Religious Affairs (Diyanet), created in 1924, runs the mosques, employs their imams, and sends out a weekly Friday sermon. The chapter compares it to the state holding the steering wheel of religion. Option C describes the American model; options A and B are not Turkish law.

questions.chapter: Day 5: The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey
questions.question_text: What happens across Turkey every November 10 at 9:05 AM?

options.A: Fireworks mark the anniversary of the Republic's proclamation
options.B: Sirens sound and the country stops for a minute of silence on the anniversary of Atatürk's death
options.C: Mosques give a special call to prayer for the soldiers of Gallipoli
options.D: Schools hold Teachers' Day ceremonies in honor of the Head Teacher

questions.explanation: Atatürk died in Dolmabahçe Palace at 9:05 AM on November 10, 1938. Every year at that moment sirens sound, and the whole country stops for a minute of silence: people stand still, drivers get out of their cars, and classes fall silent. The Republic was proclaimed on October 29, 1923 (option A). Teachers' Day (option D) falls on November 24, the day Mustafa Kemal was named Head Teacher of the Nation's Schools.

questions.chapter: Day 5: The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey
questions.question_text: Weighing the gains and costs of the alphabet reform of 1928, which judgment fits the chapter best?

options.A: It was a gain with no real cost, since the old script was used by almost no one
options.B: It failed, because adults could not learn a new script and literacy stayed at one in ten
options.C: It made reading learnable in weeks, but it was imposed from the top and cut a generation off from its written past
options.D: It was chosen by a national vote, so the losses were accepted freely by the people

questions.explanation: The new 29-letter alphabet had one letter for each sound, so a beginner could sound out any Turkish word within weeks, and literacy rose from about one in ten in 1927 to one in five by 1935. But a one-party government imposed it without a popular vote and banned the Arabic script from public use. Within a generation, most Turks could not read their grandparents' letters or the inscriptions on Ottoman fountains. Both the gain and the cost are real.

questions.chapter: Day 5: The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey
questions.question_text: In the chapter's illustrative village of 1,000 people in 1927, the same readers produce literacy rates of 9, 13, or 20 percent. What does this show?

options.A: The census takers made arithmetic mistakes that later historians corrected
options.B: Villages always have lower literacy than cities, whatever method is used
options.C: Only the lowest figure is honest, because it counts the whole population
options.D: A literacy rate depends on what counts as reading, who is in the denominator, and who did the counting

questions.explanation: Counting only readers of Ottoman Turkish over the whole population gives 9.0 percent; counting them over people aged seven and over gives about 12.9 percent; counting anyone seven or older who could read any script gives 20.0 percent. The real 1927 census also relied on self-reports with no test. So "one in ten" answers a particular question, asked by a government with a stake in the result. No method is the only honest one (option C); each answers a different question.

questions.chapter: Day 5: The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey
questions.question_text: What were the Nation's Schools (*Millet Mektepleri*)?

options.A: Free evening classes, opened in 1929, that taught adults across Turkey to read the new alphabet
options.B: Religious schools attached to mosques that taught children the Quran in Arabic
options.C: Private academies in Istanbul that trained teachers for the Ottoman court
options.D: Schools run by each millet for its own Greek, Armenian, or Jewish children

questions.explanation: The Nation's Schools opened on January 1, 1929, as free adult literacy classes meeting in the evenings in schools, coffeehouses, and village rooms, while soldiers learned in the army. Adults roughly 16 to 45 attended a few months of classes and received certificates. Mustafa Kemal was named Head Teacher, and by the government's count more than a million adults earned certificates in the first years. Despite the similar name, they had nothing to do with the millet communities' own schools in option D.

questions.chapter: Day 6: Troy and Gallipoli
questions.question_text: You stand at Schliemann's great north-south trench at Troy, reading its walls from the top down. How should you date the trench itself?

options.A: By the oldest layer it reaches, Troy I, around 3000 BCE
options.B: By the layer at its midpoint, since a trench averages the layers it crosses
options.C: As younger than every layer it cuts through, which fits its known date in the early 1870s
options.D: By the Roman marble fragments at the top, around the time of Roman Ilium

questions.explanation: Two rules read Troy's layers. The law of superposition says that in undisturbed ground a layer lies above anything older. The second rule says people dig, so a trench, pit, or foundation must be dated by the youngest layer it cuts, not the oldest material it exposes. The great trench cuts through every city, so it is younger than all of them, and we know its date: Schliemann dug it in the early 1870s. Option A makes exactly the mistake the second rule prevents.

questions.chapter: Day 6: Troy and Gallipoli
questions.question_text: Troy VI and Troy VIIa are both candidates for Homer's city. What evidence suggests that Troy VIIa, rather than Troy VI, ended in violence?

options.A: Troy VIIa has the thickest walls and the largest houses of any layer on the mound
options.B: Troy VIIa burned around 1180 BCE, with arrowheads and human remains in its ruins
options.C: Troy VIIa contains a Hittite treaty naming the king who besieged it
options.D: Troy VIIa is the layer where Schliemann found Priam's Treasure

questions.explanation: Troy VI, the grandest Troy with its sloping limestone wall, ended around 1300 BCE in damage that looks like an earthquake: collapsed walls but no great fire. The survivors rebuilt with small houses crammed against the walls and storage jars buried in the floors, like a city expecting a siege. That city, Troy VIIa, was destroyed by fire around 1180 BCE, and excavators found arrowheads and human remains. Option A describes Troy VI, and Priam's Treasure came from Troy II.

questions.chapter: Day 6: Troy and Gallipoli
questions.question_text: What is Wilusa?

options.A: The Hittite capital in central Anatolia, abandoned around 1180 BCE
options.B: The Greek name for the Mycenaean kingdom that attacked Troy
options.C: A Phoenician trading port that supplied Troy with tin
options.D: A kingdom in northwest Anatolia named in Hittite texts, which most scholars identify with Troy

questions.explanation: Wilusa is a kingdom named in Hittite texts that most scholars identify with Troy. Homer's *Ilios* was once *Wilios*, since early Greek had a *w* sound that later dropped out. Around 1280 BCE a Hittite king made a treaty with Alaksandu of Wilusa, a name strikingly like *Alexandros*, Paris's other name. The Mycenaean Greeks appear in the texts as Ahhiyawa (option B), and the Hittite capital was Hattusa (option A).

questions.chapter: Day 6: Troy and Gallipoli
questions.question_text: Troy VIIa, Hattusa, Ugarit, and the Mycenaean palaces all fell between about 1200 and 1150 BCE. Which analysis of the Bronze Age collapse best fits the chapter?

options.A: The palace systems were tightly connected, so shocks such as drought, raids, and earthquakes in one place spread into a crisis everywhere
options.B: A single invasion by the Sea Peoples destroyed every kingdom in one campaign
options.C: Iron weapons gave a new people an advantage that no Bronze Age army could match
options.D: Each kingdom collapsed for unrelated local reasons, and the shared dates are a coincidence

questions.explanation: The chapter traces a chain: drought cuts Anatolian harvests, the Hittite king depends on grain from Egypt and Ugarit, Ugarit's forces are away helping him when raiders arrive, palaces cannot pay soldiers, the tin trade stops, and earthquakes strike cities short of labor. No single cause explains it (option B), but the dates show the systems were tied together, so the palaces were strong because they were connected and fragile for the same reason. Egypt survived, so it was not universal destruction.

questions.chapter: Day 6: Troy and Gallipoli
questions.question_text: What did Milman Parry and Albert Lord discover about how oral poets like Homer could perform epics of thousands of lines?

options.A: The singers memorized a fixed text word for word, which their teachers checked against written copies
options.B: The singers stored ready-made formulas and typical scenes and recomposed the song each time, fitting phrases to the meter
options.C: The singers read from hidden scrolls, since nobody could remember so many lines
options.D: The singers improvised entirely new stories at each performance, with no repeated phrases

questions.explanation: Parry noticed that Homer's repeated phrases, like "swift-footed Achilles" or "rosy-fingered Dawn," are chosen by meter more than meaning: each formula fills a different-sized space in a line of dactylic hexameter. In 1933–1935 Parry and Lord recorded singers in Yugoslavia who did not memorize fixed texts but recomposed each song from a stock of formulas and scenes; one singer, who could not read, performed more than 12,000 lines. Option D ignores the formulas, which are the heart of the method.

questions.chapter: Day 6: Troy and Gallipoli
questions.question_text: Where does the fullest version of the Trojan Horse story come from?

options.A: The *Iliad*, which ends with the horse being dragged into Troy
options.B: A Hittite letter describing a wooden siege engine at Wilusa
options.C: Virgil's *Aeneid*, a Roman poem written around 19 BCE
