options.D: The inscriptions found in the burned layer of Troy VIIa

questions.explanation: The Trojan Horse does not appear in the *Iliad*, which ends before Troy falls. The *Odyssey* mentions it three times, briefly, as a stratagem of Odysseus. The fullest version is Virgil's *Aeneid*, written around 19 BCE, more than eleven centuries after Troy VIIa burned, where Laocoön warns, "I fear the Greeks, even bearing gifts." Historians have suggested it might remember a siege engine or an earthquake, but there is no evidence for either.

questions.chapter: Day 6: Troy and Gallipoli
questions.question_text: At Anzac Cove you read the "Johnnies and Mehmets" words attributed to Atatürk in 1934. Their earliest known source is a 1953 interview. Using the chapter's rule about the gap between an event and its evidence, how should you classify them as history?

options.A: A late or unsupported story, because the earliest evidence comes 19 years after the event
options.B: Firm history, because the words are carved on official memorials in three countries
options.C: A real core with a shaped telling, because the evidence was made within ten years
options.D: A proven forgery, because no copy from 1934 has been found

questions.explanation: The rule says evidence made at the time or within about ten years, with no reason to invent, is firm history; evidence more than ten years later makes a story late or unsupported, which may be true but cannot be shown to be. No 1934 record contains the words, and the earliest source is Şükrü Kaya's recollection in 1953, a 19-year gap. Being carved on memorials (option B) reflects cultural memory, not evidence. Missing evidence is not proof of forgery (option D).

questions.chapter: Day 6: Troy and Gallipoli
questions.question_text: Why do Turks, Australians, and Britons remember the same Gallipoli campaign so differently?

options.A: Each country was taught different facts, and historians still disagree about who won
options.B: Only the Turkish memory is accurate, because the battle was fought on Turkish soil
options.C: Britain and Australia keep their records secret, so their citizens know little of the campaign
options.D: Cultural memory keeps the parts of a shared past that help each community and retells them as its own meaning

questions.explanation: Cultural memory is how a community remembers together, through monuments, anniversaries, and school lessons, and it cares less about what happened than what the past means now. For Turks, *Çanakkale geçilmez* recalls the homeland's defense and Atatürk's rise; for Australians and New Zealanders, a national coming of age; for Britain, often a failure of command. The facts, such as the Allied withdrawal, are not in dispute (option A). Same hills, four memories, each true to its keepers.

questions.chapter: Day 6: Troy and Gallipoli
questions.question_text: You have a free afternoon in Çanakkale and want your spending to help local families. Which plan fits the chapter's advice?

options.A: Buy an extra excursion aboard the ship, since the cruise line pays local guides well
options.B: Hire a licensed local guide, eat at a family restaurant on the waterfront, and buy from a local ceramic workshop
options.C: Stay aboard and shop in the ship's boutique, which stocks Turkish goods
options.D: Visit only free sites, so that you put no strain on the town's services

questions.explanation: When a passenger buys an excursion aboard, much of the money goes first to the cruise line and its contracted operator, and the local share is mainly the coach, guide, tickets, and a souvenir stop. Hiring a licensed local guide, eating in a family restaurant, and buying from a local workshop keeps nearly all of it in Çanakkale. The excursion still buys convenience and the certainty of getting back to the ship, so the chapter suggests choosing local spending on purpose when there is a free hour.

questions.chapter: Day 6: Troy and Gallipoli
questions.question_text: The chapter compares conversational AI to a Homeric singer. Which AI tutor design best answers the risks that comparison reveals?

options.A: A tutor that writes complete answers quickly, so students finish practice problems sooner
options.B: A tutor that refuses to answer questions in a learner's own language, so they must read sources
options.C: A tutor that gives hints instead of answers, so learners still do the practice, and that points them to fixed sources to check
options.D: A tutor that gives the identical answer every time, so it never needs to be checked

questions.explanation: Like a singer, AI recomposes each answer from absorbed patterns, so a fluent answer is not a checked one, and fixed written sources still matter. And a singer became a singer through years of practice; a tool that composes for us can remove that practice. In the Turkish high-school study, students with open chatbot access did worse on later exams, while a hint-giving version removed most of the harm. Option A is exactly the open access that hurt learning.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 1: The Apostle's Life, Letters, and Ephesian Years
questions.question_text: Which list gives the seven letters that nearly all scholars agree Paul wrote himself?

options.A: Romans, Ephesians, Colossians, Galatians, Philippians, Hebrews, and Titus
options.B: Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon
options.C: Romans, 1 Corinthians, Ephesians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, and Philemon
options.D: Galatians, Ephesians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, Hebrews, and Romans

questions.explanation: The seven undisputed letters are Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon. They share a vocabulary, a style full of rhetorical questions, the same core ideas, and a situation that fits a traveling apostle of the 50s CE. The other options mix in disputed letters, such as Ephesians, Colossians, 2 Thessalonians, and the Pastoral letters, or Hebrews, which does not name its author and which scholars of all traditions agree is not Paul's.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 1: The Apostle's Life, Letters, and Ephesian Years
questions.question_text: When the Book of Acts and Paul's own letters disagree, why do historians usually give the letters priority?

options.A: Acts was written in Latin and translated badly into Greek
options.B: Acts contains no accurate local details, so none of it can be trusted
options.C: Paul's letters were checked and approved by the apostles in Jerusalem
options.D: The letters are Paul's own words from the 50s CE, while Acts came about a generation later and has its own purposes

questions.explanation: Acts, by the author of Luke's Gospel, dates to about 80–90 CE, a generation after Paul's letters. It aims to show the message moving from Jerusalem to Rome and the movement as respectable before Roman officials, and it sometimes smooths over conflicts Paul describes sharply. Option B is wrong: where Acts can be checked, its local details are often right, such as the proconsul Gallio, whose term an inscription found at Delphi dates to about 51–52 CE. So historians read it with care and prefer Paul's words.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 1: The Apostle's Life, Letters, and Ephesian Years
questions.question_text: A guide in Ephesus tells you that Paul taught daily in the hall of Tyrannus for two years. Using the chapter's four kinds of statement about Paul, which kind is this?

options.A: Something only Acts says, since Paul's letters do not mention the hall
options.B: Something Paul's own letters say, in his own voice
options.C: A later tradition added by guides and pilgrims centuries afterward
options.D: A scholars' inference drawn from both Acts and the letters together

questions.explanation: The chapter sorts every claim into four kinds: what Paul's letters say, what only Acts says, what scholars infer from both, and what later tradition adds. The hall of Tyrannus comes from Acts, which says Paul moved his teaching there from the synagogue and taught daily for two years. No building has been identified as the hall, and the "fifth to tenth hour" detail appears only in one early manuscript, the Codex Bezae. Paul's letters speak of Ephesus but never of this hall.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 1: The Apostle's Life, Letters, and Ephesian Years
questions.question_text: In every other undisputed letter, Paul follows his greeting with a thanksgiving. In Galatians he writes instead, "I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting." What can you infer from this?

options.A: Galatians was written by a follower who did not know Paul's usual letter form
options.B: The thanksgiving section was lost when the letter was copied
options.C: Paul broke the expected letter form on purpose, signaling anger and urgency that first listeners would feel at once
options.D: Paul wrote Galatians before he had learned the Greek conventions for letters

questions.explanation: A first-century listener knew how letters were supposed to go, so a missing thanksgiving would be felt at once, the way we would notice a letter that began without "Dear." Paul also calls them "foolish Galatians" and takes the pen to write in large letters at the end. Form, tone, and handwriting all say the letter is urgent: other teachers were telling his non-Jewish converts to be circumcised and keep the law. Galatians is undisputed, which rules out option A.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 1: The Apostle's Life, Letters, and Ephesian Years
questions.question_text: Acts claims that during Paul's Ephesian years "all the residents of Asia" heard the message. How could this be roughly true even though Paul stayed in Ephesus?

options.A: Paul walked to every city in the province during his two to three years there
options.B: The Roman governor ordered all the province's cities to send delegates to hear Paul
options.C: Pilgrims to the Temple of Artemis were required to attend Paul's lectures
options.D: From the capital and port, co-workers went out along the roads, and visitors came in on business, so churches grew across the province

questions.explanation: Ephesus was the provincial capital, its biggest port, and a road hub, and the Temple of Artemis drew pilgrims. Paul's letters show how the message spread without him: Epaphras, a native of Colossae, founded communities in the Lycus valley about 170 km inland; Philemon of Colossae probably met Paul in Ephesus; and Paul sends greetings from "the churches of Asia." A single base with co-workers and visitors could reach a whole province in two or three years. No source says Paul traveled the whole province.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 1: The Apostle's Life, Letters, and Ephesian Years
questions.question_text: Acts says three times that Paul was a Roman citizen, but his own letters never mention it and say he was "beaten with rods" three times. How should you describe his citizenship to a fellow traveler?

options.A: "Paul was definitely a Roman citizen, because Acts is our only narrative of his life."
options.B: "Acts says Paul was a citizen; his letters don't, and the question can't be settled from the evidence."
options.C: "Paul was definitely not a citizen, because citizens were never beaten by officials."
options.D: "Paul bought his citizenship from a tribune in Jerusalem for a large sum."

questions.explanation: Being beaten with rods was a Roman punishment a citizen was supposed to be spared, so some historians doubt the citizenship. Others reply that provincial officials did not always respect the law, or that Paul chose not to claim his rights. Because the evidence cannot settle it, the guide itself says "Acts says Paul was a citizen." Option D confuses Paul with the tribune Claudius Lysias, who in Acts says he bought his citizenship, while Paul says he was born a citizen.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 1: The Apostle's Life, Letters, and Ephesian Years
questions.question_text: Paul's own letters describe his call in a few words, while Acts tells the road-to-Damascus scene three times with shifting details. What can a historian say with confidence?

options.A: Paul fell from his horse when a bright light struck him, exactly as painters show
options.B: Nothing at all, because the accounts disagree
options.C: Paul believed the risen Jesus had appeared to him, and it changed his life; the scene's details come from Acts' retellings
options.D: Paul was blinded for three years and went to Jerusalem only after his sight returned

questions.explanation: Paul's letters say only that God "was pleased to reveal his Son to me" and that Jesus "appeared also to me," with no light, fall, or blindness. Acts' three tellings share a core, a light, a voice, and a commission, but shift details to suit each audience, as ancient historians did. So a historian can say Paul believed he had seen the risen Jesus and that it changed his life. The horse in option A comes from neither source; it entered the story through painters such as Caravaggio.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 1: The Apostle's Life, Letters, and Ephesian Years
questions.question_text: Who were the "God-fearers" that Acts mentions?

options.A: Gentiles drawn to Judaism's one God and its moral teaching who did not become Jews
options.B: A strict group of Pharisees who refused to eat with Gentiles
options.C: Priests of Artemis who protected the temple's treasury at Ephesus
options.D: Paul's opponents in Galatia who demanded that converts be circumcised

questions.explanation: Gentiles are people who are not Jewish, and in Ephesus they were the great majority. Some were drawn to Judaism's single God and its moral teaching without becoming Jews, and Acts calls them God-fearers. Inscriptions near our route show the term was real: a donor list at Aphrodisias names donors called *theosebeis*, "God-worshippers," separately from Jewish donors, and a theater seat at Miletus is usually read as reserved for Jews "who are also God-fearers."

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 1: The Apostle's Life, Letters, and Ephesian Years
questions.question_text: Many scholars think the Pastoral letters (1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, and Titus) were written after Paul's death. Which evidence gives the strongest case for that view?

options.A: The letters are addressed to individuals rather than to whole communities
options.B: They use many words found nowhere else in Paul and describe settled church offices that fit the next generation
options.C: Churches today read them less often than the seven undisputed letters
options.D: They mention Timothy and Titus, who could not have known Paul personally

questions.explanation: The case is strongest for the Pastorals because several independent lines of evidence agree: a large share of vocabulary found nowhere else in Paul, a church with settled offices of overseers, elders, and deacons with written qualifications, and "the faith" as a fixed body of teaching to guard. Option A is weak, since Philemon is also personal and undisputed. Option D is false: Timothy and Titus were Paul's co-workers who carried his letters. Use in churches (option C) says nothing about authorship.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 1: The Apostle's Life, Letters, and Ephesian Years
questions.question_text: Koine Greek let Paul's letters travel without translators. How does the chapter compare that with what AI translation offers learners today?

options.A: AI translation works exactly like Koine, by persuading everyone to learn one common language
options.B: AI translation removes every risk, because no language can be crowded out once machines translate
options.C: Koine spread ideas more widely than AI translation ever could, since machines cannot translate meaning
options.D: Learners can keep their own language and still reach ideas in any other, though large languages may crowd out small ones

questions.explanation: Alexander's conquests made Koine the common tongue, so Paul could write in one language to Galatians, Corinthians, and Romans. Instead of everyone learning one common language, AI translation lets each learner keep their own and still reach ideas written in any other, a real lowering of the cost of learning. It carries a familiar risk: a few large languages may crowd out small ones, as Koine slowly crowded out Anatolia's old languages. That rules out options A and B.

questions.chapter: Day 7: Ephesus, a Greco-Roman City
questions.question_text: Why does ancient Ephesus now stand several kilometers from the sea, with its old harbor a field?

options.A: The Cayster River carried soil down every winter and dropped it at its mouth, pushing the coast west
options.B: An earthquake raised the land and drained the harbor in a single day
options.C: The Romans filled in the harbor to build Marble Street and the theater
options.D: The sea level of the Aegean has fallen steadily since Roman times

questions.explanation: Ephesus harbor silting was the slow filling of the harbor with mud carried by the Küçük Menderes, the Cayster of the Greeks. Its winter floods dropped soil where the current slowed, so the coastline crept west and the city chased it. The archaic city stood near the Temple of Artemis, Lysimachus refounded it around 290 BCE nearer the water, and Byzantine and Turkish Ayasuluk took over as the harbor failed. The chapter describes a gradual process, not a single earthquake.

questions.chapter: Day 7: Ephesus, a Greco-Roman City
questions.question_text: Statues of Artemis of Ephesus have a mass of rounded, egg-shaped objects on the chest. What do scholars actually know about them?

options.A: They are breasts, as an ancient inscription at the temple explains
options.B: They are bees, the symbol of the city on its coins
options.C: They are the eggs of the griffins shown on her skirt
options.D: No ancient text explains them, so their meaning is unknown

questions.explanation: Visitors are often told the objects are breasts, but they have no nipples, and scholars have proposed eggs, gourds, the testicles of sacrificed bulls, or amber ornaments sewn onto a garment. No ancient text explains them, so the honest answer is that we do not know. The bee was one of her symbols, but it appears among the animals on her skirt and on coins, not as the objects on her chest. She was likely an older Anatolian mother goddess under a Greek name.

questions.chapter: Day 7: Ephesus, a Greco-Roman City
questions.question_text: At the Basilica Stoa, you see a column standing on a molded base, with a pair of spiral scrolls on its capital. Which order is it?

options.A: Doric, because it has a plain cushion-shaped capital
options.B: Ionic, because it has a base and volutes on its capital
options.C: Corinthian, because it has acanthus leaves around a tall bell
options.D: Tuscan, because it is the plainest of the Roman orders

questions.explanation: Reading a column from the bottom up, the molded base rules out Doric, which has no base. The pair of spiral scrolls, called volutes, on the capital makes it Ionic, the order born in Ionia on this coast. A Corinthian capital is a tall bell wrapped in acanthus leaves, and Doric has a simple cushion under a square slab. The chapter's rule of thumb: base, shaft, capital, and entablature are four questions, and the capital alone usually answers the main one.

questions.chapter: Day 7: Ephesus, a Greco-Roman City
questions.question_text: Near the Prytaneion you pass the ruined Memmius Monument, carved with figures in relief. Its inscription names Gaius Memmius, a grandson of the Roman dictator Sulla. What does reading that inscription add to your visit?

options.A: It gives the exact date the monument fell in an earthquake
options.B: It proves the monument was moved here from Rome
options.C: It identifies whom the monument honored and reveals who held power in the city
options.D: It lists the craftsmen who carved the relief figures

questions.explanation: Inscriptions are Ephesus's richest primary sources: they name who paid, who was honored, and why. Without its inscription, the Memmius Monument would be just a handsome ruin. With it, we know it honored the grandson of Sulla, who had punished the cities of this province after the massacre of 88 BCE. A monument to the dictator's grandson in the heart of Ephesus tells us who held power here. The chapter does not say the inscription dates its fall or names its carvers.

questions.chapter: Day 7: Ephesus, a Greco-Roman City
questions.question_text: Why does a true fresco, like those in the terrace houses, last so much better than ordinary paint?

options.A: The colors were mixed with oil, which seals the wall against water
options.B: Pigments in water are applied to wet lime plaster, and as it dries the color is bound into the wall itself
options.C: The painting was baked in a kiln before being set into the wall
options.D: A layer of glass tesserae was laid over the paint to protect it

questions.explanation: "Fresco" is Italian for "fresh." The painter coats the wall in lime plaster and, while the top layer is still wet, applies pigments mixed with water. As the lime dries, a chemical reaction binds the color into the surface, so a true fresco does not flake off like surface paint and lasts as long as the plaster. Because only as much wall is plastered as can be painted before it sets, large frescoes were made in daily patches whose joins can sometimes be seen. Glass tesserae make a mosaic, not a fresco.

questions.chapter: Day 7: Ephesus, a Greco-Roman City
questions.question_text: Every local detail in Acts' story of the silversmiths' riot fits what the inscriptions of Ephesus say. What does that evidence allow us to conclude?

options.A: The author knew how Ephesus worked, though that does not prove every word of the scene happened as told
options.B: The riot happened exactly as told, including every word of the town clerk's speech
options.C: Acts must have been written by an Ephesian official who kept the city's records
options.D: The story was invented, because accurate details are what a skilled forger would include

questions.explanation: Details such as the town clerk, the Asiarchs, and Ephesus as temple warden of Artemis match the city's own inscriptions, which shows the author knew how Ephesus worked. But Acts was written a generation later, and its speeches are the author's own composition, so the match does not prove every word happened as told (option B). Accurate background makes the story plausible rather than proven, and nothing in the evidence points to an official author or to forgery.

questions.chapter: Day 7: Ephesus, a Greco-Roman City
questions.question_text: From the lower part of the site, your guide points to a square stone tower on a western hilltop called St. Paul's Prison. How should you describe it?

options.A: The cell where Acts says Paul was held before the silversmiths' riot
options.B: A Byzantine chapel built over the place where Paul was executed
options.C: A modern replica built for pilgrims in the 20th century
options.D: A real tower from Lysimachus' Hellenistic city wall, whose link to Paul is tradition only

questions.explanation: The tower is real and old: it was part of the city wall built by Lysimachus in the early 3rd century BCE. The identification with Paul is tradition only. Acts mentions no imprisonment in Ephesus, which rules out option A, though Paul's own letters lead many scholars to think he was imprisoned somewhere in the province. Even so, nothing ties him to this tower, which was a fortification, not a jail or a chapel. It is a real Hellenistic tower with a name added much later.

questions.chapter: Day 7: Ephesus, a Greco-Roman City
questions.question_text: What did the Council of Ephesus, meeting in the Church of Mary in 431 CE, decide?

options.A: That the Temple of Artemis should be closed and its stones reused for churches
options.B: That the Book of Acts and Paul's letters should be added to the Bible
options.C: That Mary could rightly be called *Theotokos*, "God-bearer," because Jesus was one person, both God and man
options.D: That Ephesus, not Jerusalem, was the place where Mary was buried

questions.explanation: Summoned by Theodosius II and counted as the third great council, it met in the Church of Mary in 431. Nestorius of Constantinople preferred "Christ-bearer" to keep Jesus' human and divine natures distinct, while Cyril of Alexandria insisted that because Jesus was one person, his mother could be called the bearer of God. The council, led by Cyril, upheld *Theotokos*, which became a central Orthodox title of Mary. The council made no ruling on Mary's burial place.

questions.chapter: Day 7: Ephesus, a Greco-Roman City
questions.question_text: How did the Asia Minor refugees of 1922–1923 change Greece?

options.A: About 1.2 million people arrived in a country of about five million, founding new neighborhoods and bringing music such as rebetiko and Anatolian dishes
options.B: They stayed only a few years and then returned to their homes in Anatolia
options.C: They settled mainly on the islands of the Dodecanese, which were empty at the time
options.D: They were absorbed so quickly that they left no trace on Greek culture

questions.explanation: About 1.2 million Greek Orthodox refugees arrived in a country of about five million, and many lived for years in tents and shacks. New neighborhoods around Athens and Piraeus were named for lost homes, such as Nea Smyrni and Nea Ionia, and others settled farmland in northern Greece. They brought the music that grew into rebetiko, dishes such as *soutzoukakia smyrneika*, and skills in trade and crafts. The exchange was compulsory and permanent, so none could return (option B).

questions.chapter: Day 7: Ephesus, a Greco-Roman City
questions.question_text: Compare Aquila's gift of the Library of Celsus with Andrew Carnegie's libraries. Which analysis of their designs fits the chapter?

options.A: Both donors paid all costs forever, so neither library ever depended on its city
options.B: Aquila's library failed because he gave no money for books, while Carnegie's succeeded because he bought every book
options.C: Carnegie's libraries were open to all readers, while the Library of Celsus allowed only scholars inside
options.D: Carnegie required towns to pay yearly upkeep, which spread libraries and kept towns invested, while Aquila endowed books and upkeep, which lasted only as long as his money

questions.explanation: Aquila left 25,000 denarii to buy books and maintain the building, so his library ran on his own money and then depended on the city. Carnegie paid for more than 2,500 buildings but required each town to provide the land and pay about a tenth of his gift yearly for books, staff, and upkeep, so the idea spread and towns stayed invested. Option B reverses the facts. Neither went all the way: a library serves only those who can read and reach its door.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change
questions.question_text: What did the leaders of the early Jesus movement decide at the Council of Jerusalem, about 48 or 49 CE?

options.A: That Jewish believers must stop keeping the law of Moses
options.B: That Paul alone would lead the mission to the Gentiles, without consulting Jerusalem
options.C: That Gentile believers did not have to be circumcised or take on the whole Jewish law
options.D: That the movement would separate from Judaism and found a new religion

questions.explanation: Acts 15 and Galatians 2 tell the meeting differently, but they agree on the core: Gentiles could belong without circumcision. In Acts, James adds four rules, which Paul never mentions. For Jewish believers the law remained their way of life; the decision was about what could not be imposed on newcomers, so option A reverses it. The chapter calls it the movement's first recorded decision about what was essential and what was not, made by deciding what to stop requiring.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change
questions.question_text: Livy tells a fable of limbs that refuse to feed the belly; Paul uses the same body image in 1 Corinthians 12. How does Paul change its moral?

options.A: Livy's fable tells the common people to keep serving the powerful, while Paul says the weaker members are indispensable and honored
options.B: Paul uses it to tell the poor to return to work, just as the Roman senator did
options.C: Paul replaces the body with a building, so the image has nothing in common with Livy's
options.D: Both use it to argue that every member of a community should hold the same gift

questions.explanation: In Livy's story, the senator Menenius Agrippa persuaded Rome's protesting common people to return by telling of limbs that starved themselves by refusing to feed the belly: the hands should keep serving. Paul wrote to Corinthians who ranked one another by their gifts and left the poor hungry at shared suppers. He says the eye cannot tell the hand "I have no need of you," the weaker members are indispensable, and "if one member suffers, all suffer." Same image, opposite direction.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change
questions.question_text: How did the Protestant Reformation grow out of a reading of Paul?

options.A: Augustine nailed theses about Galatians to a church door in Milan in 386
options.B: The Council of Trent ordered every priest to preach only from Paul's letters
options.C: John Wesley translated Romans into German in 1738, starting the Lutheran church
options.D: Martin Luther, lecturing on Romans, came to read righteousness as God's gift and issued his 95 Theses in 1517

questions.explanation: Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar teaching the Bible at Wittenberg, lectured on Romans in 1515 and 1516 and came to read "the one who is righteous will live by faith" as a promise that God gives righteousness as a gift. On October 31, 1517, he issued his 95 Theses against the sale of indulgences, and printing spread his pamphlets within weeks. Augustine's 386 moment was a conversion in a Milan garden, and Wesley, two centuries later, heard Luther's preface to Romans read aloud.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change
questions.question_text: Paul wrote a harsh passage about Jews in 1 Thessalonians, yet in Romans 9 to 11 he pictured Gentile believers as branches grafted onto Israel's olive tree. How does the chapter analyze the role of his words in Christian anti-Judaism?

options.A: Paul's letters contain no harsh lines, so later anti-Judaism had no connection to them
options.B: His words point in more than one direction, and later Christians quoted the harsh lines while forgetting the olive tree
options.C: Paul intended to found a church that replaced Israel, so later anti-Judaism simply followed his plan
options.D: The harsh lines appear only in the disputed letters, so they can be set aside as not his

questions.explanation: In Romans 9 to 11, Paul writes of "great sorrow" for his people, asks whether God has rejected them, answers "By no means!", and warns Gentiles that "the root supports you." But the harsh passage in 1 Thessalonians, an undisputed letter, is also his, so option D fails. From John Chrysostom to Luther, Christians quoted the harsh lines and forgot the olive tree. After the Holocaust, churches began to repudiate "the teaching of contempt," and *Nostra Aetate* drew on Paul's olive tree.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change
questions.question_text: Why does the chapter treat the Carnegie unit as an inherited form rather than an essential purpose of schooling?

options.A: It was created in 1906 for pensions and transcripts, and it counts hours in class rather than learning
options.B: It was invented by Andrew Carnegie to measure how well students read
options.C: It requires every student to master a subject before earning credit
options.D: It was abolished in 1906, so modern schools no longer use it

questions.explanation: The Carnegie unit, defined in 1906 as 120 hours of class in one subject over a year, was created to decide which colleges qualified for the Carnegie Foundation's pensions and to give colleges a common way to read transcripts. Most American high schools still award credit on that basis. Its weakness is that it counts seat time, not learning, so a student who already knows the material and one who is lost earn the same credit. That is the opposite of mastery (option C).
questions.concept: Seat Time and the Carnegie Unit

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change
questions.question_text: A school district wants to spread an AI-native model to many schools but has only a small team. Following Paul's Ephesian strategy, what should it do?

options.A: Send the team to visit every school once a year for a short training day
options.B: Launch the model in all schools at the same moment so no school feels left out
options.C: Establish the model firmly at one well-connected pilot school that others already visit, and let visitors and co-workers carry it home
options.D: Wait until a national mandate requires every school to change at once

questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke diffusion establishes a change firmly at one central place, then lets people who travel between places carry it outward. Paul stayed in Ephesus, where roads, ships, courts, and festivals brought people anyway, while co-workers such as Epaphras carried the message to Colossae, Laodicea, and Hierapolis, places Paul never visited. A leader who chooses the hub well does not have to go everywhere. The pilot school as hub applies the same idea; option A spreads a small team too thin.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change
questions.question_text: Around 112 CE, the Roman governor Pliny reported that once he had suppressed the Christians, temples filled again and sacrificial meat began selling. What does this evidence add to the story of Demetrius the silversmith?

options.A: It proves that the riot in Ephesus happened word for word as Acts tells it
options.B: It shows that Demetrius invented the threat to his trade in order to attack Paul
options.C: It shows that Roman governors supported the Christians against the old cults
options.D: It confirms from an independent pagan source that the old cults' economy shrank where the movement grew, so Demetrius' resistance was rational

questions.explanation: The economics of resistance holds that people resist change partly because of what it costs them: income, skill, status, and identity. Acts, a Christian history, and Pliny, a pagan governor writing to Trajan, independently describe the same pattern: where the new movement grew, the old cults' trade shrank. So Demetrius was right about his market. The lesson for schools is to treat a teacher's fear for her job as a legitimate concern that deserves a straight answer, not to call it irrational.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change
questions.question_text: Three months into an AI-tutoring pilot, the share of questions students answer correctly has fallen from 70 to 63 percent. What does the idea of the implementation dip advise?

options.A: Cancel the pilot at once, since the new method has clearly made students worse
options.B: Expect a temporary drop while people build new skills, and stay with the change, as Paul stayed with Corinth
options.C: Hide the results from teachers so that they do not lose confidence
options.D: Return to the old method for three months, then try the new one again from the start

questions.explanation: Michael Fullan found that before people are fluent in a new practice, they are worse at it than at the old one. In the illustrative pilot, scores fall to 63 percent by month three, pass the baseline by month six, and reach 78 percent by month twelve, so a leader who judges the pilot at month three cancels it just before the payoff. Corinth was Paul's dip: factions and lawsuits a year or two in. He did not abandon it; he wrote, sent Timothy, visited, and wrote again.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change
questions.question_text: A principal must choose one teacher to champion a new approach among cautious colleagues. Which choice fits the chapter's advice?

options.A: The respected veteran who was skeptical at first and changed her mind publicly, given protected time and a lighter load
options.B: The newest teacher, who is most excited about technology and has no old habits to unlearn
options.C: An outside consultant who has led the change in many other districts
options.D: The biggest enthusiast on staff, asked to take on the role on top of a full teaching load

questions.explanation: Like Paul, a Pharisee who knew the law and had opposed the movement, an insider change leader carries credibility outsiders lack. Veteran teacher champions are the school's version: colleagues believe someone like themselves, so the respected skeptic who changed her mind publicly persuades better than the biggest enthusiast. The outside consultant who "flies in for a day" lacks that credibility. Champions also need protected time and a lighter load, or the first adopter burns out, which rules out option D.

questions.chapter: Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change
questions.question_text: The chapter admits the Paul parallel has limits. Which judgment best explains why a school leader cannot simply copy Paul's approach?

options.A: Paul's letters are too old to say anything useful about organizations today
options.B: Paul's mission failed, so its strategies should be avoided
options.C: Schools change faster than first-century communities, so patience is no longer needed
options.D: Paul's hearers chose to join and needed no data, while students cannot opt out and a school must show a change helps and be ready to stop

questions.explanation: Among the limits the chapter lists, Paul believed he carried a message from God, and his hearers chose to join and could leave. Students and teachers in a public school do not choose most changes made to it. Paul also had no data and needed none, while a school must show that a change helps students and be ready to stop if it does not. The chapter still finds the case study useful, which rules out options A and B.

questions.chapter: Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights
questions.question_text: What does the Greek word *philoxenia* mean, and why did it carry special weight in ancient Greece?

options.A: "Love of wisdom," because philosophers were honored guests in every city
options.B: "Fear of foreigners," because strangers were thought to bring disease
options.C: "Friendship among citizens," because only citizens could share a meal
options.D: "Love of the stranger," a religious duty protected by Zeus Xenios

questions.explanation: *Philoxenia* joins *philos*, "loving," and *xenos*, a word meaning both "stranger" and "guest." In ancient Greece hospitality was a religious duty: Zeus himself, as *Zeus Xenios*, protected travelers and punished those who mistreated them. Homer's *Odyssey* is built on the custom, and the suitors who abuse Odysseus's hospitality die for it. The custom lives on in the fruit or sweet a taverna brings that nobody ordered. "Love of wisdom" (option A) is philosophy.

questions.chapter: Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights
questions.question_text: At the entrance to Mandraki harbor, a fellow traveler points to the two bronze deer and says the Colossus once stood with one foot on each column. What is the best reply?

options.A: Yes, and ships sailed between its legs until the earthquake of 226 BCE
options.B: Probably not: a bronze statue that tall could not stand with its legs so far apart, and it more likely stood on land, though no one knows where
options.C: Yes, because the deer columns were built on the statue's original foundations
options.D: No, because the Colossus was never built; it existed only in legend

questions.explanation: The famous engravings show the Colossus astride the harbor mouth, but a bronze statue about 33 m tall could not have stood with its legs that far apart, and the entrance was far too wide. Scholars think it more likely stood on land, near the harbor or in a sanctuary of Helios higher in the city; no one knows. It was real, though (option D): Chares of Lindos built it, it stood about 54 years, and Pliny the Elder saw the fallen pieces.

questions.chapter: Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights
questions.question_text: A museum case shows a silver coin with a woman's head in a crested helmet on one side and, on the other, an owl, an olive sprig, and the letters ΑΘΕ. What are you looking at?

options.A: A Rhodian coin showing the sun god Helios
options.B: A Roman coin showing the goddess of war, Minerva
options.C: An Athenian silver tetradrachm showing Athena, the coin traders called "owls"
options.D: A Spartan coin showing Artemis the huntress

questions.explanation: A god is identified by attributes. A helmet alone could mean any war deity, but the owl and the olive together settle it: Athena, whose sacred animal was the little owl and whose gift to Athens was the first olive tree. The letters ΑΘΕ read *A-TH-E*, short for "of the Athenians." So this is an Athenian silver tetradrachm, the coin traders across the Mediterranean simply called "owls." Rhodes's own god Helios was a sun god, not a helmeted goddess.

questions.chapter: Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights
questions.question_text: What set the Rhodes School of Rhetoric apart from the other famous styles of its day?

options.A: It taught a middle way between the plain Attic style and the ornate, emotional Asian style
options.B: It taught only the plain, spare style of Athens and banned emotion from speeches
options.C: It taught in Latin, so Roman students did not need to learn Greek
options.D: It taught rhetoric through writing alone, with no speeches in front of an audience

questions.explanation: The Attic style, named for Athens, was plain and spare; the Asian style, popular in cities such as Ephesus, was ornate, rhythmic, and emotional. Rhodes stood between them on the map and in taste: rich enough to move an audience, controlled enough to be trusted. Its most famous teacher, Apollonius Molon, reined in the young Cicero's overflowing delivery. Molon listened to students speak and made them do it again, which rules out option D, and Cicero declaimed to him in Greek.

questions.chapter: Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights
questions.question_text: What does a label stating "acidity ≤ 0.3%" tell you about a bottle of extra virgin olive oil?

options.A: The oil has been refined with heat and chemicals to remove its acid
options.B: The oil is too acidic to be sold as extra virgin, which requires at least 1%
options.C: Its free acidity is well under the 0.8% limit for extra virgin, a sign of sound, quickly milled olives
options.D: The oil was made from unripe olives, which are always lower in fat

questions.explanation: Free acidity measures how much the oil has broken down; it rises when olives are bruised, overripe, or left too long before milling. EU rules require 0.8% or less for extra virgin, so 0.3% is well inside the limit. Option B reverses the rule: a bottle at 1.5% could not be extra virgin. The best grades need no heat or chemicals. The chapter's other tips: look for a harvest date such as "2026/27" and choose dark glass or a tin.

questions.chapter: Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights
questions.question_text: Inside the Palace of the Grand Master you admire grand halls and Hellenistic floor mosaics. How should you date most of what you are seeing?

options.A: As the knights' original 14th-century palace, preserved untouched since 1522
options.B: As an Ottoman palace built for the island's governors after the siege
options.C: As a Byzantine citadel that the knights only repainted
options.D: As an Italian reconstruction of 1937–1940 on medieval foundations, with mosaics brought from Kos

questions.explanation: The knights built the palace in the 14th century on a Byzantine citadel, but in 1856 lightning ignited gunpowder stored in the nearby Church of St. John, and the explosion wrecked much of the palace. The Italian governor rebuilt it from 1937 to 1940 as a residence for the king of Italy and Mussolini, filling it with mosaics brought from Kos. It is a good museum, but it is mostly a 1930s reconstruction on medieval foundations, a case for Chapter 4's restoration-versus-reconstruction test.

questions.chapter: Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights
questions.question_text: After the siege of 1480, why did the knights rebuild the walls of Rhodes lower and much thicker, with projecting bulwarks?

options.A: Tall, thin medieval walls shatter under cannon fire, so walls had to absorb shot and let defenders fire along their face
options.B: An earthquake had toppled the tall walls, and there was no stone left to rebuild them to their full height
options.C: The Ottomans had agreed by treaty to attack only low walls
options.D: Lower walls were cheaper, since the order had lost most of its income

questions.explanation: The new problem after 1480 was cannon. Tall, thin medieval walls shatter under cannon fire, so the knights made the walls lower and much thicker, built massive bulwarks that projected outward so defenders could fire along the wall face, and widened the moat. The dry moat was a killing ground, trapping attackers between the outer and main walls. Each tongue held its own stretch. The chapter gives no earthquake, treaty, or money reason for the redesign.

questions.chapter: Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights
questions.question_text: The knights surrendered Rhodes to Suleiman in December 1522. Why could both sides tell the outcome as a victory?

options.A: The knights kept the island, while Suleiman received a yearly payment of tribute
options.B: The knights left with their arms and honor and the inhabitants kept their faith, while Suleiman ended a costly siege and won the island intact
options.C: Christian Europe sent a fleet that forced a draw, so neither side lost
options.D: Suleiman released all his prisoners, and the knights agreed never to fight again

questions.explanation: A city taken by storm could expect to be sacked and its people killed or enslaved. Instead the knights surrendered on terms: they left with their arms, relics, and honor, inhabitants could go with them, and those who stayed kept their faith and churches. Suleiman ended a siege that had cost him enormous losses and gained the island intact. No help came from Christian Europe (option C), and the knights sailed out on January 1, 1523, later holding Malta against another Ottoman siege in 1565.

questions.chapter: Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights
questions.question_text: Crete's Muslims all left in the 1923 population exchange, yet Rhodes still has a small Turkish-speaking Muslim community. What explains the difference?

options.A: The Muslims of Rhodes converted to Orthodox Christianity before 1923
options.B: The treaty exempted all islands with more than one mosque
options.C: Rhodes's Muslims spoke Greek, and the exchange sorted people by language
options.D: The exchange applied only to Greece and Turkey, and in 1923 Rhodes belonged to Italy

questions.explanation: The 1923 exchange swapped the Orthodox of Turkey for the Muslims of Greece, but in 1923 Rhodes belonged to neither country: Italy had held it since 1912. So the island's Muslims were not exchanged, and they are Greek citizens today, some still worshipping in their own mosques. The Dodecanese joined Greece only by the 1947 treaty. Option C is wrong twice: the exchange sorted people by religion, not language, and this community's home language is Turkish.

questions.chapter: Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights
questions.question_text: In 1944 a registry list of Jewish residents, prepared for a "routine check," helped the deportation find every family on Rhodes. What lesson does the chapter draw for AI tutors?

options.A: Schools should never keep any records about their students
options.B: AI tutors are dangerous and should not be used in schools
options.C: Learner data is not neutral: collect only what teaching needs, control who sees it, and plan for a change in who is in charge
options.D: Student data is safe as long as it is collected for an ordinary purpose

questions.explanation: Records made for ordinary purposes, a census, a school roll, a registry, became the tool that found every family in July 1944. The Jews of Rhodes were murdered by people who chose to murder them, but the list made it fast and complete. An AI tutor collects detailed information about each student, so the chapter's safeguards are to collect only what teaching needs, control access, and plan for new people in charge. Option D is exactly the assumption the 1944 list disproves.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 1: Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B
questions.question_text: On the Grand Staircase at Knossos you see red columns that are wider at the top than at the bottom, holding up an upper floor. How should you read what is in front of you?

options.A: As original Minoan wooden columns, preserved by the fire that ended the palace
options.B: As Arthur Evans's reconstruction, mainly in reinforced concrete from the 1920s, painted in the Minoan column shape
options.C: As a Roman rebuilding of the palace for visitors in the 2nd century CE
options.D: As a modern copy built after 2000 to replace stone columns that collapsed

questions.explanation: The palace's wooden columns and beams had burned or rotted away, so Evans rebuilt rooms, stairways, and upper floors between about 1905 and 1930, first with wood and stone and from the 1920s mainly in reinforced concrete. His architects rebuilt the Grand Staircase and painted concrete columns red, in the Minoan shape that widens toward the top. So the site must be read as three things together: Minoan remains, Evans's rebuilding, and modern copies. No original wooden column survives.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 1: Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B
questions.question_text: Evans called the gypsum seat in the Throne Room "the throne of Minos." What does the chapter say we actually know about it?

options.A: King Minos sat there, as an inscription on the seat records
options.B: It was brought from mainland Greece by the Mycenaeans as war booty
options.C: The seat is original and in place, but the room's present form dates after about 1450 BCE, and who sat there is unknown
options.D: It is a concrete copy made by Evans, since the original seat was destroyed

questions.explanation: The high-backed gypsum seat is one of the few things in the palace exactly where the Bronze Age left it, so option D is wrong. But the room in its present form dates from the last phase, after about 1450 BCE, when Mycenaeans ruled Knossos. Who sat there is unknown; some scholars suggest a priestess appearing as a goddess between her guardian griffins, which fits the many Minoan images of powerful women and the absence of any clear image of a king. No inscription names Minos.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 1: Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B
questions.question_text: How did the palace economy of Knossos work?

options.A: The palace collected produce and labor, stored and recorded them, and paid them out as rations, wages, and offerings
options.B: Farmers sold their olive oil in a central market and paid the palace a tax in silver coins
options.C: Each village kept its own harvest, and the palace traded only in foreign luxuries
options.D: Merchants owned the storerooms and rented space to the palace officials

questions.explanation: The palace economy worked by redistribution: goods flowed into a center and back out, directed by officials, rather than being bought and sold in a market. A village's share of olive oil arrived in jars, a scribe recorded it on a clay tablet, and the jars went into the west storerooms. Later the oil went out as rations to workers, raw material for perfume makers, and offerings to the gods, each issue with its own tablet. No market sale was involved, which rules out option B.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 1: Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B
questions.question_text: In 1939 Spyridon Marinatos proposed that the Thera eruption destroyed Minoan civilization. Why has better dating changed that verdict?

options.A: The eruption turned out to be small, leaving only a thin layer of ash on Thera
options.B: The eruption happened after the palaces were already abandoned, around 1100 BCE
options.C: Akrotiri was found to be a Mycenaean town, so its loss did not affect the Minoans
options.D: The palaces carried on for more than a century after about 1600 BCE, so the eruption weakened Minoan Crete but did not end it

questions.explanation: The Thera eruption, around 1600 BCE, was one of the largest of the last ten thousand years. It buried the Minoan-style town at Akrotiri, ash fell on eastern Crete, and debris suggests a tsunami reached the north coast, so the claim that it weakened Minoan Crete is likely. But the palaces carried on for more than a century afterward, and most were destroyed about 1450 BCE, so the claim that it destroyed Minoan civilization is not supported. Option A contradicts the eruption's enormous scale.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 1: Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B
questions.question_text: In the Heraklion museum you stand before a complete-looking Minoan fresco, bright from edge to edge. What should you assume about it?

options.A: It was lifted whole from a palace wall, where the ash of Thera protected it
options.B: It is a modern painting with no ancient material in it
options.C: It is a reconstruction: real fragments set into new plaster, with the missing areas painted in by a restorer
options.D: It was repainted by the Mycenaeans after they took over Knossos

questions.explanation: Almost no Minoan paintings survived on the walls. They fell when the palaces burned and collapsed and came out of the ground as heaps of small fragments, so every fresco in the museum is a reconstruction of real fragments in new plaster. The "Saffron Gatherer," restored as a boy picking crocuses, turned out to be a blue monkey. The ash of Thera protected paintings at Akrotiri, not at Knossos, which rules out option A. Option B goes too far, since real fragments are included.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 1: Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B
questions.question_text: What is the firmest evidence that a place called the Labyrinth really existed at Mycenaean Knossos?

options.A: A Linear A tablet that draws a map of the maze beneath the palace
options.B: A Linear B tablet recording an offering of honey to "the Mistress of the Labyrinth"
options.C: Homer's description of Daedalus building the maze for King Minos
options.D: The double axes carved on the palace blocks, which prove the name means "house of the double axe"

questions.explanation: A Linear B tablet from Knossos records an offering of honey to "the Mistress of the Labyrinth," so a place or shrine with that name existed at Mycenaean Knossos. The link between "labyrinth" and the *labrys*, the Minoan double axe, is popular, but linguists are divided on it, so option D overstates it. The myth of the Minotaur and the maze was written down centuries after the palace fell. Linear A is undeciphered, so no tablet in it can be read as a map.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 1: Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B
questions.question_text: Linear A is undeciphered, yet scholars agree that the word *ku-ro* means "total." How did they work this out?

options.A: A bilingual tablet gave the Greek word for "total" beside it
options.B: Michael Ventris guessed it from a Greek word that sounds similar
options.C: *Ku-ro* is written in large letters, so it must be the most important word on each tablet
options.D: The number after *ku-ro* at the bottom of account tablets equals the sum of the numbers above it

questions.explanation: Many Linear A signs look like Linear B signs with known sounds, so scholars can sound out *ku-ro* without knowing the Minoan language. Its meaning came from arithmetic: on account tablets from Hagia Triada, the number after *ku-ro* at the bottom equals the sum of the entries above. A scribe's habit of adding up a column told more than staring at the signs. Linear A has no bilingual text and no strong guess about its language, which is why it remains unread.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 1: Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B
questions.question_text: What makes the Phaistos Disc unique among ancient texts?

options.A: Its signs were pressed into wet clay with carved stamps, making it the oldest known text printed with reusable "type"
options.B: It is the longest Minoan text ever found, with thousands of signs
options.C: It is the bilingual tablet that allowed Linear B to be deciphered
options.D: It was written in the Greek alphabet centuries before Homer

questions.explanation: The Phaistos Disc, found in 1908 and usually dated to about 1700 BCE, carries 241 signs of 45 kinds in a spiral on both sides. Each sign was pressed into the wet clay with a carved stamp, one stamp per kind, so it is the oldest known text printed with reusable type, more than 3,000 years before Gutenberg. But it is the only object with these signs, and 241 signs are far too few to decipher, so it is neither long (option B) nor a key to Linear B.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 1: Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B
questions.question_text: A school plans to run all of its core teaching on one company's AI system, with student work stored in that company's formats. Applying the lesson of Linear B, what should the school do?

options.A: Proceed as planned, since a large company is unlikely to fail
options.B: Avoid AI entirely, since any shared tool will eventually be lost
options.C: Spread the knowledge widely, keep work in open formats, keep teachers skilled in what the machines do, and know how to leave
options.D: Restrict the AI to a few trusted staff so the knowledge stays under close control

questions.explanation: Linear B, held by a few dozen palace scribes for one narrow purpose, vanished when the palaces fell. The modern form is concentrated AI risk: teaching held inside one company's system can be lost, priced out of reach, or controlled overnight. The defenses are the ones the scribes lacked: spread knowledge widely, keep it in open formats, keep teachers skilled, and know how to leave. Option D repeats the scribes' mistake by concentrating knowledge in a few hands.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 1: Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B
questions.question_text: Why does the chapter insist that the decipherment of Linear B be told with Alice Kober in it?

options.A: She was the first to read Linear B as Greek, before Ventris
options.B: Her years of groundwork on about 180,000 index cards revealed the script's structure, and Ventris used her method
options.C: She found the Pylos tripod tablet that proved the decipherment
options.D: She controlled the Knossos tablets and published them all in her lifetime

questions.explanation: Kober refused to guess the language and instead found its structure from sign patterns, building her own database of about 180,000 hand-cut index cards. Her "triplets" showed the language was inflected and that signs were syllables sharing consonants or vowels, the start of the grid. Ventris read the script as Greek in 1952 using her method, but for decades the story was told as his alone. Credit for groundwork matters today too, for the people who label AI training data. Blegen found the Pylos tablet, and Evans controlled the Knossos texts.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 2: Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today
questions.question_text: Where does the name "Candia," which the Venetians used for Heraklion and for all of Crete, ultimately come from?

options.A: From the Arabic *Rabdh al-Khandaq*, "the castle of the moat," the fortified town the Arabs built in the 820s
options.B: From the Latin word for "white," after the island's limestone cliffs
options.C: From the name of the Minoan palace's harbor recorded on Linear B tablets
options.D: From the Turkish *Kandiye*, given by the Ottomans after 1669

questions.explanation: The Arabs who took Crete in the 820s built a fortified town protected by a great ditch and called it *Rabdh al-Khandaq*, "the castle of the moat." After the Byzantine reconquest of 961 the Greeks called it Chandax, the Venetians turned that into Candia, and the Ottomans into Kandiye, so option D reverses the order. In the 19th century Greeks revived the ancient name Herakleion, after a harbor of Knossos. Each ruler renamed the place, and the Arab moat set the line later walls followed.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 2: Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today
questions.question_text: Inside the Church of Agios Titos, you notice a broad, open, domed hall, filled with icons. Which history explains what you see?

options.A: It was always an Orthodox church, built in this shape to copy Hagia Sophia
options.B: It was built by the Venetians as a Catholic cathedral and never changed hands
options.C: It was a church, then a mosque rebuilt after an 1856 earthquake, and became an Orthodox church again in 1925
options.D: It was built as a mosque in 1925 and later given to the Orthodox Church

questions.explanation: Agios Titos records every ruler in the chapter. It was first built after the Byzantine reconquest of 961, became a Catholic church under Venice and a mosque under the Ottomans, and was rebuilt as a mosque after an earthquake destroyed it in 1856. It served Heraklion's Muslims until they left in the 1923 population exchange, and in 1925 it was consecrated as an Orthodox church again. That is why its domed hall keeps the broad, open shape of a mosque, now filled with icons.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 2: Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today
questions.question_text: Why are the bastions of Heraklion's Venetian walls shaped like arrowheads rather than round towers?

options.A: Arrowhead shapes used less stone, which was scarce on Crete
options.B: The shape copied the Minoan double axe, the ancient symbol of Crete
options.C: Pointed bastions could ram enemy ships that came too close to the shore
options.D: Guns on each bastion's flanks fire along the faces of its neighbors, so no dead ground is left for attackers

questions.explanation: Defenders on a round tower cannot see the foot of their own tower or much of the wall between towers; that hidden "dead ground" is where attackers place ladders or dig mines. An arrowhead bastion's two short flanks carry guns that fire sideways along the faces of the neighboring bastions and the wall between, so each bastion covers the next and every meter of the ditch is under fire. Draw the lines of fire, and the arrowhead is the shape left when no dead ground remains.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 2: Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today
questions.question_text: How did the twenty-year Siege of Candia end in 1669?

options.A: The city was stormed and sacked, and every defender was killed
options.B: Francesco Morosini negotiated an honorable surrender: the garrison and inhabitants could leave with their property
options.C: A French army broke the siege, and Venice kept Crete until 1913
options.D: The Ottomans gave up and sailed home after a plague struck their camp

questions.explanation: The Ottomans dug in before Candia in 1648, and the city held for more than twenty years, supplied by sea, in a war of mines and countermines. After the grand vizier Köprülü Fazıl Ahmed Pasha took command and a French expedition failed, Morosini negotiated a surrender in September 1669. The terms were generous: the garrison and any inhabitants who wished could leave with their property, and Venice kept three small island fortresses. Ottoman Crete followed until 1898.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 2: Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today
questions.question_text: At the lion fountain in Lions Square, a fellow traveler says, "The Morosini who built this later blew up the Parthenon." How should you correct them?

options.A: The fountain was built by the Ottomans, and Morosini only repaired it
options.B: Nobody named Morosini was ever involved with the Parthenon
options.C: The fountain's builder was the doge of Venice, who never visited Crete
options.D: The fountain was built in 1628 by the governor Francesco Morosini, a different man from the namesake who surrendered Candia and led the army that hit the Parthenon in 1687

questions.explanation: The Morosini Fountain was built in 1628 by the Venetian governor Francesco Morosini at the end of an aqueduct bringing water from Mount Juktas. He is easy to confuse with his namesake, Francesco Morosini (1619–1694), who commanded Candia late in the siege, surrendered it in 1669, and in 1687 led the Venetian army whose shell blew up the Parthenon. So option B is wrong too: a Morosini did hit the Parthenon, just not this one. The square is officially Venizelou Square, but everyone calls it "the Lions."

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 2: Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today
questions.question_text: Which statement about El Greco is supported by the chapter?

options.A: Born in Candia in 1541, he trained as an icon painter in the Cretan tradition before working in Venice, Rome, and Toledo
options.B: He was a Spanish painter who moved to Crete late in life and painted its monasteries
options.C: His most famous paintings hang in Heraklion, where he worked all his life
options.D: He was a Venetian governor of Crete who painted as a hobby

questions.explanation: El Greco, "the Greek," was Domenikos Theotokopoulos, born in Candia in 1541. He trained as an icon painter in the Cretan tradition, was a master painter there by 1563, moved to Venice about 1567, to Rome in 1570, and settled in Toledo in 1577. He signed in Greek letters, sometimes adding *Kres*, "Cretan." His famous canvases, such as *The Burial of the Count of Orgaz*, are in Spain; Heraklion's Historical Museum holds two small paintings, which rules out option C.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 2: Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today
questions.question_text: Virgil's works run to about 12,900 lines. An Aldine-style octavo fits 30 lines on each page and 16 pages on each sheet. About how many sheets of paper does each copy need?

options.A: About 215 sheets
options.B: About 27 sheets
options.C: About 54 sheets
options.D: About 430 sheets

questions.explanation: At 30 lines a page, 12,900 ÷ 30 = 430 pages, and at 16 pages to a sheet, 430 ÷ 16 is about 26.9, so 27 sheets. Option D confuses pages with sheets. Option A is the chapter's folio edition with commentary: 15 lines a page gives 860 pages, and at 4 pages a sheet, 215 sheets. So the octavo carries every line of Virgil on about one-eighth of the paper, and since handmade paper was one of the largest costs, the price fell with it.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 2: Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today
questions.question_text: Why does the chapter call the Battle of Crete in May 1941 a turning point in the history of warfare?

options.A: It was the last battle in which cavalry charged against tanks
options.B: It was won by Cretan villagers alone, without any Allied troops
options.C: It was the first large invasion carried out mainly from the air, and German paratrooper losses were so heavy that Hitler never ordered another
options.D: It was the first battle in which submarines landed an invading army

questions.explanation: On May 20, 1941, German paratroopers and glider troops landed around the north-coast airfields and towns. They took terrible losses, but once they held the airfield at Maleme, reinforcements flew in, and within about ten days the Allies were evacuating to Egypt. German losses among their elite paratroopers were so heavy that Hitler never again ordered a large airborne operation. British, Australian, New Zealand, and Greek troops fought alongside Cretan civilians, so option B is wrong.

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 2: Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today
questions.question_text: Which two forces does the chapter say shaped the traditional Cretan diet?

options.A: Poverty and the land, and the Orthodox calendar of fasting from meat, dairy, and eggs
options.B: Venetian trade in spices, and Ottoman palace cooking
options.C: Modern nutrition research, and the tourist demand for healthy food
options.D: The Minoan palace economy, and the rations of the Battle of Crete

questions.explanation: Farm families ate what their own fields, trees, flocks, and hillsides gave them, with meat kept for feast days. The Orthodox fasting calendar asks the faithful to give up meat, dairy, and eggs on most Wednesdays and Fridays and through long seasons; the Nativity fast begins on November 15, so late-November menus mark *nistisima*, fasting dishes. A cuisine that must feed people well without animal products becomes very good at vegetables, pulses, and olive oil. Researchers recorded the diet in the mid-20th century; they did not create it (option C).

questions.chapter: Day 9, Part 2: Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today
questions.question_text: Aldus's pocket classics were cheap, but his privileges made the printers of Lyon who copied them into pirates. What does this contrast show about open educational resources?

options.A: Cheap books and open resources are the same thing, so Aldus already made his books open
options.B: Open licenses are dangerous because they let anyone spread errors, so they should be avoided
options.C: Low prices alone guarantee that everyone can learn, so licenses do not matter
options.D: An open license turns copiers into partners who spread and fix a text, and because copies then cost nothing, careful editing matters more

questions.explanation: Affordable course materials lower the price; open educational resources also carry a license that lets anyone copy, adapt, translate, and share. Aldus's books were cheap but not open, so under an open license the Lyon printers would have been partners, spreading the text and fixing its errors. When copies cost nothing, an editor's mistakes multiply as freely as the truth, as Musurus's did in 1513. The chapter's answer is more careful editing, not avoiding openness (option B).

questions.chapter: Day 10: Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars
questions.question_text: Which description of Herodotus is supported by the chapter?

options.A: An Athenian general who fought at Marathon and wrote a diary of the battle
options.B: A Roman historian who translated Persian records into Latin
options.C: A Spartan poet who sang the Persian Wars in the style of Homer
options.D: A writer born a Persian subject at Halicarnassus, whose *Histories* present his *historia*, "inquiry"

questions.explanation: Herodotus was born about 484 BCE at Halicarnassus, modern Bodrum, so he grew up a subject of the Persian king. His *Histories*, finished around 430 BCE, open by presenting his *historia*, Greek for "inquiry," the source of our word *history*. He names his sources, gives Persian, Phoenician, and Greek versions side by side, and reports what people say without believing all of it. Cicero called him the father of history. It was the playwright Aeschylus, not Herodotus, who fought at Marathon.

questions.chapter: Day 10: Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars
questions.question_text: Herodotus says Xerxes' land army had 1,700,000 infantry. How does the chapter suggest we treat that number?

options.A: As reported rather than believed, since feeding it would take about 1,700 tonnes of grain a day, and modern estimates are far smaller
options.B: As exact, since Herodotus copied it from the Persian army's own records
options.C: As proof that his whole account of the war is invented and should be ignored
options.D: As too small, since modern historians think the Persians brought even more men

questions.explanation: At about 1 kg of grain per soldier per day, 1.7 million soldiers would eat about 1,700 tonnes a day, roughly 50,000 tonnes a month, all moved along one coast road. Working from what roads, water, and food could support, modern historians usually estimate about 100,000 to 300,000 fighting men. So we keep Herodotus' account of what happened and where, and treat his numbers the way he treated his own sources: reported, not believed. Doubting one figure does not mean discarding the whole history (option C).

questions.chapter: Day 10: Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars
questions.question_text: A tour guide at Marathon says a runner carried news of the victory to Athens, cried "We have won!", and died. Applying the myth test to the sources, what should you conclude?

options.A: It is firm history, because Herodotus describes the run in detail
options.B: The death-run is a legend first written 550 to 650 years later; the real feat was Pheidippides' run of about 240 km to Sparta before the battle
options.C: It is a modern invention made up for the first Olympic marathon in 1896
options.D: It is firm history, because the length of the modern marathon matches the road from Marathon to Athens

questions.explanation: Herodotus, writing about 60 years after the battle, tells of a runner named Pheidippides who ran from Athens to Sparta before the battle to ask for help, about 240 km in two days. He never mentions a death-run to Athens. That story first appears in Plutarch and Lucian, 550 to 650 years after the battle. So the real feat is the one fewer people know. The race distance of 42.195 km is a modern convention set for London in 1908, not evidence about 490 BCE.

questions.chapter: Day 10: Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars
questions.question_text: What lesson does the chapter draw from Herodotus for students who use AI systems?

options.A: Trust an AI answer if it is written in smooth, confident prose
options.B: Avoid AI entirely, because it cannot write history as well as Herodotus did
options.C: Ask of any answer "Who says so? How do they know? What do other sources say?", the habit of *historia*
options.D: Prefer poets and royal inscriptions, since they record the past most faithfully

questions.explanation: Before Herodotus, the past was told by poets singing what the Muses gave them and by kings carving what they wished remembered, neither inviting questions. Herodotus wrote in prose and showed his work: who told him what, what he saw, and where sources disagreed. An AI system usually answers in one smooth, confident paragraph without separating sourced facts, passed-on reports, and its own conclusions. A student who asks "Who says so?" is practicing *historia*, which rules out option A.

questions.chapter: Day 10: Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars
questions.question_text: Pericles said Phidias' statue of Athena Parthenos carried 40 talents of refined gold, all removable. If an Attic talent weighed about 26 kg, roughly how much gold was on the statue?

options.A: About 1,040 kg, roughly a tonne
options.B: About 66 kg, the weight of an adult
options.C: About 400 kg, less than half a tonne
options.D: About 10,400 kg, more than ten tonnes

questions.explanation: Forty talents at about 26 kg each gives 40 × 26 = 1,040 kg, roughly a tonne of gold. Thucydides reports that Pericles counted it among the city's emergency reserves, to be borrowed and replaced. The removable design also protected Phidias: Plutarch says that when enemies accused him of stealing gold, the plates were taken off and weighed, and the charge failed. Option B adds the numbers instead of multiplying them, and option D is ten times too large.

questions.chapter: Day 10: Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars
questions.question_text: What is the most surprising feature of the Parthenon's geometry?

options.A: Every block is identical, so damaged pieces can be swapped easily
options.B: It was laid out exactly on the golden ratio in every dimension
options.C: It has no columns on its long sides, only solid walls
options.D: Almost nothing in it is straight: the platform rises toward the middle, and the columns lean inward and swell slightly

questions.explanation: The Parthenon's platform rises gently toward the middle of each side, about 6 cm on the ends and 11 cm on the long sides, so it does not look as if it sags. Its columns lean slightly inward and swell a little in the middle, a curve called *entasis*, and the corner columns are a bit thicker. Because every block was cut for its own place, no two are quite alike, which rules out option A. The chapter says it was built on a 4-to-9 proportion, not the golden ratio.

questions.chapter: Day 10: Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars
questions.question_text: You photograph the six Caryatids holding up the Erechtheion's south porch. What are you actually looking at?

options.A: The original statues, cleaned with lasers and returned to the porch in 2009
options.B: Statues of women from Caryae, carved as a punishment, as the building's accounts record
options.C: Copies put in place in 1979; five originals are in the Acropolis Museum and the sixth is in the British Museum
options.D: Roman replacements made after the originals were destroyed in 1687

questions.explanation: The Caryatids on the building are copies, put in place in 1979 to save the originals from air pollution. Five originals stand in the Acropolis Museum, cleaned with lasers, and the sixth is in London, taken by Lord Elgin's agents. Option B fails the myth test: the punishment story comes from Vitruvius, while the Erechtheion's own building accounts simply call the statues *korai*, "maidens," and the name may come from Caryae's dances for Artemis.

questions.chapter: Day 10: Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars
questions.question_text: Why do Greek and Turkish kitchens share so many dishes, often under nearly the same names?

options.A: Both countries adopted the same French cookbooks in the 20th century
options.B: The two peoples lived in one empire for centuries, and the 1923 exchange carried Anatolian cooking to Greece
options.C: Turkish cooks copied Greek recipes when Greece ruled Istanbul in the 1800s
options.D: The dishes all come from ancient Athens and spread east with Alexander

questions.explanation: Greeks and Turks lived in one empire for centuries, and the population exchange of 1923 sent refugees west with their cooking: *soutzoukakia smyrneika*, meatballs with cumin, are named for Smyrna. Who invented each dish is argued with feeling in both countries, a gentle case of contested history. Moussaka has an Arabic-derived name and versions across the Ottoman world, and coffee reached Istanbul from Yemen. The chapter's answer is that each dish belongs to everyone who cooked it. Greece never ruled Istanbul (option C).

questions.chapter: Day 10: Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars
questions.question_text: In the Parthenon Marbles dispute, which statement belongs to the agreed facts rather than to the disputed meaning?

options.A: The sculptures belong in London because more visitors can see them there
options.B: The sculptures belong in Athens because they are part of one building
options.C: Elgin's permission was clearly illegal under Ottoman law
