options.D: Between 1801 and 1812 Elgin's agents removed about half the surviving sculpture, and the original permission document has never been found

questions.explanation: The dispute is contested history: the basic facts are largely agreed, and the argument is over what they mean and where the sculptures should be. Agreed facts include that Elgin's agents removed about half the surviving sculpture between 1801 and 1812, while Athens was Ottoman, and that the original permission document has never been found, though an Italian translation survives. Options A and B are the two sides' positions, not facts. Option C states a conclusion the agreed facts do not settle.

questions.chapter: Day 10: Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars
questions.question_text: What is the difference between hubris and hamartia in Greek tragedy?

options.A: Hubris is arrogant overreaching that invites ruin; hamartia is an error or mistake, often made in ignorance
options.B: Hubris is a mistake made in ignorance; hamartia is arrogant pride against the gods
options.C: Both words mean the same "tragic flaw" that every hero has
options.D: Hubris is a type of chorus song; hamartia is the final scene of a tragedy

questions.explanation: Hubris is arrogant overreaching, pride that exceeds human limits or treats the gods' order with contempt; in Athenian law it was also a crime of humiliating assault. Herodotus' Xerxes, who had the Hellespont lashed, fits the pattern. Aristotle's word for what brings a hero down is *hamartia*, an error or mistake, often in ignorance, as when Oedipus does not know his parents. The chapter warns against treating hubris as every hero's "tragic flaw" (option C), and option B swaps the two.

questions.chapter: Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus
questions.question_text: Why is the Temple of Hephaestus above the Agora the best-preserved temple of the classical Greek world?

options.A: It was buried by a landslide and dug out whole in the 20th century
options.B: It was rebuilt in concrete by Arthur Evans's architects in the 1920s
options.C: It became a Christian church dedicated to St. George and was used as one until 1834
options.D: It was built of bronze rather than marble, so it could not be burned for lime

questions.explanation: The Temple of Hephaestus, begun around 449 BCE, honored the god of fire and the forge and overlooked a district of foundries and potters. It survived almost whole because it became a Christian church dedicated to St. George and was used as one until 1834. Standing beside it, we see a Doric temple with its columns, entablature, and pediments still whole. Its continuous use, not burial or a modern rebuilding, is what saved it, metopes of Heracles and Theseus included.

questions.chapter: Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus
questions.question_text: What made Athenian democracy direct rather than representative?

options.A: Citizens decided in person in the Assembly, and councillors and jurors were chosen by lot rather than elected
options.B: Citizens elected a parliament that made laws on their behalf for ten-year terms
options.C: A single elected leader governed with the advice of a council of priests
options.D: All residents of Attica, including women and enslaved people, voted on every law

questions.explanation: From 508 to 322 BCE, every adult male citizen could attend, speak, and vote in the Assembly, which met about 40 times a year on the Pnyx. There was no elected parliament. The Council of 500, which prepared the agenda, was chosen by lot for one year, and juries of hundreds were chosen by lot on the morning of a trial. The city paid citizens for public service so the poor could take part. But women, metics, and enslaved people had no vote, which rules out option D.

questions.chapter: Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus
questions.question_text: Excavators found about 190 ostraka with Themistocles' name, written by only a few hands and never used. What can you infer from this find?

options.A: Themistocles wrote the ballots himself to prove how popular he was
options.B: Someone organized a campaign against him, and some voters needed ready-made ballots because they could not write
options.C: Ostracism votes were always rigged, so the system never reflected real opinion
options.D: The ballots were practice pieces from a school where children learned to write

questions.explanation: Ostracism exiled a leading politician for ten years by a vote scratched on potsherds. Ballots prepared in a few hands, apparently to hand out, show that someone was organizing a campaign against Themistocles, and that some voters needed a ballot already written because they could not write the name themselves. A democracy that voted in writing quietly assumed a literacy not every citizen had. One find of unused ballots does not show every vote was rigged (option C).

questions.chapter: Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus
questions.question_text: Why does the chapter warn against reading the trial of Socrates in 399 BCE as "democracy versus philosophy"?

options.A: Socrates was tried by a Spartan court, not by the Athenian democracy
options.B: Socrates was acquitted, and the death sentence is a later legend
options.C: The charge was only about unpaid taxes and had nothing to do with religion
options.D: Athens had just lost a war and suffered the Thirty Tyrants, and philosophy went on flourishing there for centuries afterward

questions.explanation: Athens lost the Peloponnesian War in 404 BCE, and the Thirty Tyrants ruled by terror until 403; their leader Critias had been Socrates' companion. Because an amnesty barred prosecutions for acts under the Thirty, an impiety charge could carry an unspoken political one. Socrates had questioned Athenians for decades, his students kept teaching, and Athens remained the philosophy capital for nine centuries. A jury of about 500 citizens convicted him, and he drank hemlock about a month later.

questions.chapter: Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus
questions.question_text: Which idea was part of the Stoic teaching that Zeno began in the Painted Stoa around 300 BCE?

options.A: Pleasure is the highest good, so a wise person seeks a quiet, comfortable life
options.B: All humans share in reason, so every person is a citizen of one world, a *kosmopolitēs*
options.C: Health, wealth, and reputation are the true goods that make a life happy
options.D: The gods do not exist, so the world runs by pure chance

questions.explanation: Zeno of Citium taught in the Painted Stoa, which gave the Stoics their name, "the porch people." Three Stoic ideas matter here: the world is ordered by reason, the *logos*; virtue is the only good, while health, wealth, and reputation are "indifferent," which rules out option C; and all humans form one community, since every person shares in reason, making each a *kosmopolitēs*, the source of "cosmopolitan." The Stoics often called that rational force god or Zeus, so option D is wrong.

questions.chapter: Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus
questions.question_text: Both Epictetus and Paul use the Stoic word for contentment. How do their reasons for being content differ?

options.A: Epictetus is content because he is wealthy, while Paul is content because he is poor
options.B: Both find their strength in the same source, the divine reason inside every person
options.C: For the Stoic, contentment comes from within, wanting only what is up to him; for Paul, from outside, "the one who strengthens him"
options.D: Epictetus rejected contentment as a goal, while Paul made it the center of his teaching

questions.explanation: Epictetus would say a wise person is content because he wants only what is up to him, his own judgments, so nothing outside can take his peace. Writing to the Philippians from prison, Paul uses the same Stoic word, *autarkēs*, but says he can do all things through the one who strengthens him. Same word, similar circumstances, opposite source of strength. That pattern, borrowed vocabulary carrying a new meaning, is exactly what Paul does on the Areopagus.

questions.chapter: Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus
questions.question_text: On the Areopagus, a guide tells you that archaeologists found the very altar inscribed "To an unknown god" that Paul mentions. How should you weigh that claim?

options.A: Accept it, because Acts is the earliest source and names the altar exactly
options.B: Reject the whole story, because no Greek ever built an altar to an unnamed god
options.C: Accept it, because the bronze plaque on the hill marks the altar's original spot
options.D: No such altar has been found; independent writers attest altars to unknown gods in the plural, and only Acts has the singular

questions.explanation: No altar with exactly that wording has been found in Athens. Pausanias and Philostratus independently describe altars to unknown gods, plural, and Jerome thought Paul turned a plural into a singular to suit his argument. So altars to unknown gods are well attested, which rules out option B, but the singular form appears only in Acts. The bronze plaque carries the text of the speech in Greek; it does not mark an altar. Either way, Paul starts from something the listeners built.

questions.chapter: Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus
questions.question_text: A teacher hearing about a new AI tutor asks, "Will I be able to do this?" Using the stages of concern, which response fits best?

options.A: Offer a smaller first step that answers her worry about her own ability
options.B: Give her a long presentation on research showing the tutor's effect on test scores
options.C: Tell her the decision has been made and her concerns do not matter
options.D: Wait until she stops asking questions before introducing the tool

questions.explanation: The Concerns-Based Adoption Model, developed by Gene Hall, Shirley Hord, and colleagues, finds that concerns move from the self, to the task, to the impact on others. A leader helps most by answering the concern a person actually holds. *AI-Native Schools* pairs "Will I be able to do this?" with a smaller first step, a classroom visit with "What does it look like?", and coaching with "How do I fit it in?" Research on student impact (option B) answers a later concern she does not yet hold.

questions.chapter: Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus
questions.question_text: What does the ancient symposium show about the chapter's larger theme?

options.A: That Athenian women led the city's philosophy, since they hosted the parties
options.B: That wine was always drunk unmixed, as a sign of Greek refinement
options.C: That brilliant conversation belonged to free citizen men, while women came as hired musicians and enslaved servants filled the cups
options.D: That every Athenian, rich or poor, attended a symposium each evening

questions.explanation: The symposium, "drinking together," followed dinner in a Greek house. Male guests reclined on couches, wine was mixed with water in a *krater*, since unmixed wine was thought barbaric (option B), and talk, songs, and games followed. Plato's *Symposium* has Socrates outtalk everyone. But the women present were hired musicians and companions, and enslaved servants filled the cups. It shows the chapter in miniature: brilliant conversation within a narrow circle. Tonight's open taverna table is a democratic improvement.

questions.chapter: Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus
questions.question_text: A skilled craftsman in Athens earned about 1 drachma a day, and a mina was 100 drachmas. Evenus of Paros charged 5 minae to teach virtue. How many days of a craftsman's wages was that?

options.A: About 5 days
options.B: About 50 days
options.C: About 100 days
options.D: About 500 days, well over a year of work

questions.explanation: Five minae at 100 drachmas each is 500 drachmas, and at about 1 drachma a day that is about 500 days of a craftsman's wages, well over a year of work. That figure comes from Plato's *Apology*. Option A forgets to convert minae to drachmas. A much later report says Protagoras charged 100 minae, more than 25 years of wages, though that may be exaggerated. Either way, a Sophist's course was out of reach for any working family, while Socrates charged nothing.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 1: The Oracle
questions.question_text: According to the chapter, what three things make a statement a real prediction?

options.A: It makes a claim, it is made before the outcome, and some possible outcome could prove it wrong
options.B: It comes from a god, it is spoken in verse, and it is recorded by a priest
options.C: It states a probability, it uses numbers, and it is made by an expert
options.D: It gives advice, it is easy to remember, and it comes true in the end

questions.explanation: A prediction makes a claim about something not yet known, is made before the outcome, and can be checked: some outcome could show it to be wrong. A forecast adds a stated likelihood, and a prophecy is a prediction said to come from a god, so neither probability nor divine origin is required (options B and C). Many statements that sound like predictions are really commands or advice. The chapter's motto: a prediction has to be able to lose.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 1: The Oracle
questions.question_text: Using the chapter's three-part test, which of these statements is a real prediction?

options.A: "If you make war, you will destroy a great empire."
options.B: "Found a city in Libya."
options.C: "Know thyself."
options.D: "It will rain at Delphi tomorrow afternoon."

questions.explanation: "Rain at Delphi tomorrow afternoon" makes a claim before the outcome, and a dry afternoon would prove it wrong, so it can lose. The Croesus answer (option A) is hedged: it comes true whether Lydia or Persia wins, so it predicts nothing. "Found a city in Libya" is a command that tells us what to do, not what will happen. "Know thyself" is advice carved on the temple porch. Only option D passes all three parts of the test.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 1: The Oracle
questions.question_text: Joseph Fontenrose sorted about 535 recorded Delphic responses by how close the record was to the event. What pattern did he find?

options.A: The answers recorded closest to the event were mostly elaborate riddles in verse
options.B: The answers recorded closest to the event were mostly short, practical commands and approvals, while the famous riddles cluster in later stories
options.C: Almost every recorded answer turned out to be a forgery written by Roman authors
options.D: The oracle answered only state questions, never private ones

questions.explanation: Fontenrose found that the answers recorded nearest the time are mostly short and practical, such as "it is better to sacrifice to this god" or "yes, the law is approved." The famous double-edged riddles cluster in stories written down later. Scholars still argue about individual judgments, but the shape of the result has held: the riddling oracle of legend and the practical oracle of the inscriptions are not the same. Most consultations were in fact private, which rules out option D.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 1: The Oracle
questions.question_text: Apply the chapter's "both outcomes" test to the oracle's answer that no one was wiser than Socrates. What does it show?

options.A: It is a hedge, because it comes true whether or not a wiser person exists
options.B: It is a command, because it tells Socrates to become wise
options.C: It could lose, since finding someone wiser would prove it false, so it makes a real claim
options.D: It is meaningless, because wisdom cannot be measured at all

questions.explanation: The test lists the possible outcomes and asks which would make the answer true. For Croesus, both a Lydian and a Persian victory make it true, so it cannot lose. For Socrates, finding someone wiser would make the answer false, so it could lose. That is why Socrates spent decades trying to prove the god wrong, questioning politicians, poets, and craftsmen. He found each thought he knew things he did not. Option A wrongly treats it like the Croesus answer.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 1: The Oracle
questions.question_text: Before Salamis, the oracle told Athens that a "wooden wall" alone would not fall and spoke of "divine Salamis." Analyzing how Athens used the answer, which conclusion fits the chapter?

options.A: The oracle told the Athenians exactly what to do, and they simply obeyed
options.B: The professional interpreters read the answer correctly, and the Assembly followed them
options.C: The answer was so clear that no debate was needed
options.D: The Assembly chose between rival readings and voted for Themistocles' view that "divine" meant the dead would be the enemy's and the wall was the fleet

questions.explanation: In the Assembly, some said the wooden wall meant the old thorn hedge around the Acropolis; the professional interpreters said "divine Salamis" foretold an Athenian defeat at sea. Themistocles argued that a god meaning Athenian deaths would have said "cruel," not "divine," so the wall was the ships. The Assembly voted with him. The Athenians needed both the god's answer and their best forecaster's judgment, and the decision was still theirs. Herodotus wrote about fifty years later, and some suspect the answer was polished afterward.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 1: The Oracle
questions.question_text: During an oracle consultation, how did the priests test whether Apollo was present that day?

options.A: They sprinkled a goat with cold water; if it trembled through its whole body, the god was present
options.B: They watched whether the sacred flame in the temple burned blue
options.C: They asked the Pythia to name a stranger she had never met
options.D: They listened for thunder from Mount Parnassus at dawn

questions.explanation: The consultation steps are pieced together from Plutarch, Herodotus, Euripides, inscriptions, and the temple layout. Consultants arrived on a consultation day, purified with water from the Castalian Spring, and paid the fee, the *pelanos*, with foreigners presented by a Delphian sponsor, a *proxenos*. Then the priests sprinkled a goat with cold water. If it trembled through its whole body, Apollo was present and consultations could go ahead; if not, there would be none that day.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 1: The Oracle
questions.question_text: Herodotus reports that the Pythia Perialla was bribed to say Demaratus was not a true king's son, and that she was removed from office when the plot came out. What does this case reveal about the oracle?

options.A: The oracle was a fraud from the start, so no Greek trusted it again
options.B: Bribery was legal at Delphi, since the priests openly sold favorable answers
options.C: The oracle could be corrupted through human hands, but when found out it punished its own
options.D: Only foreign kings, never Greeks, ever tried to influence the Pythia

questions.explanation: Around 491 BCE, the Spartan king Cleomenes had a powerful Delphian, Cobon, persuade the Pythia to declare that Demaratus was not the true son of the previous king. When the plot came out, Cobon fled and Perialla was removed. The story shows both the flaw and a defense against it. Greeks kept consulting the oracle for centuries, so option A is wrong, and the Spartans and the Athenian Alcmaeonids, who were both Greek, were the bribers, so option D is wrong too.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 1: The Oracle
questions.question_text: De Boer and Hale argued that ethylene rising through faults beneath the temple inspired the Pythia. Weighing the evidence, which judgment is best supported?

options.A: The theory is proven: measured ethylene levels at Delphi are high enough to cause a trance
options.B: Ancient writers reported a vapor and the faults are real, but the gas is disputed, since later measurements found little or no ethylene
options.C: The theory is a hoax, because there are no faults anywhere near Delphi
options.D: The question is closed, because ancient writers never mentioned anything rising from the ground

questions.explanation: Strabo describes a breath rising from a cave, and Plutarch mentions a sweet smell and a weakening vapor, so option D is wrong. De Boer and Hale showed that two faults cross beneath the temple and that a nearby spring held traces of light gases, so option C is wrong. But later measurements found little or no ethylene, and critics argued a trance would need far more gas than any plausible leak. Two of three claims hold; the gas itself is still debated.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 1: The Oracle
questions.question_text: How did the meaning of "Know thyself," carved on the temple porch, change over six centuries?

options.A: It always meant "know your enemies," as generals understood it
options.B: It began as Plato's call to self-examination and later became a warning about mortal limits
options.C: It was a password that let paying visitors into the inner room of the temple
options.D: It moved from "know you are a mortal, not a god," to Socrates' self-examination, to Plutarch's reading as the god's reply, "you are not"

questions.explanation: In the Archaic age, scholars think it meant: know that you are mortal, and know your limits before approaching Apollo. Around 380 BCE, Plato's Socrates turned it inward, toward examining one's own beliefs and ignorance. Around 100 CE, a speaker in Plutarch's *The E at Delphi* read it as the god's reply to a worshipper's "you are": you are not. Option B reverses the order. The sayings were free advice for everyone, read before anyone paid for an answer.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 1: The Oracle
questions.question_text: We visit Delphi on November 22. In the oracle's great days, what would we most likely have found?

options.A: The god away for the winter and the Pythia silent, with Dionysus holding the sanctuary
options.B: The busiest consultation day of the year, on Apollo's birthday
options.C: A special winter oracle given only to foreign visitors
options.D: The Pythia answering daily, since consultations ran every day of the year

questions.explanation: Greeks believed Apollo left Delphi for the three winter months, usually to the Hyperboreans "beyond the north wind," and the oracle gave no answers while Dionysus held the sanctuary. Greek months were lunar and cannot be converted exactly, but the silence is generally put from about November or December to February, so we would very probably have found the god away. Apollo's birthday fell in Bysios, in early spring, which rules out option B, and consultations were monthly at most, not daily.

questions.chapter: Day 12: Delphi
questions.question_text: You arrive at Delphi in late morning after a two-and-a-half-hour drive, and the sun sets about 5:15 PM. What is the best way to plan your visit?

options.A: See everything on the site and in the museum, since a full day is plenty of time
options.B: Decide before arriving which three or four things matter most, since an hour on the site is not enough to linger everywhere
options.C: Skip the museum entirely, since the originals are all on the site
options.D: Start at the stadium and work down after dark, when the site is quieter

questions.explanation: The day trip is about 180 km and two and a half hours each way. Our own photos on the site span about an hour, enough to walk the Sacred Way to the temple and theater at a steady pace but not to linger. Add the museum, which deserves at least an hour, plus lunch, and much of the drive home is in the dark. The museum holds originals such as the Charioteer, so skipping it (option C) would miss them.

questions.chapter: Day 12: Delphi
questions.question_text: What was the real job of the more than twenty treasuries along the Sacred Way?

options.A: They were banks where pilgrims deposited money for safekeeping
options.B: They were lodgings for envoys waiting to consult the oracle
options.C: They were schools where priests trained the Pythia
options.D: They held a city's offerings and stood in the god's precinct with the city's name on them, advertising its wealth and piety

questions.explanation: A treasury was not a bank (option A). These small, temple-shaped buildings held gifts of gold, silver, and bronze, ritual equipment, and spoils of war, but their real job was to stand in Apollo's precinct with their city's name on them. Rival cities lined the Sacred Way with them. The Corinthian treasury held Croesus' gifts, and Siphnos built its marble treasury around 525 BCE with young women holding up its porch. Most are now only foundations.

questions.chapter: Day 12: Delphi
questions.question_text: Pausanias says the Athenian Treasury was built from the spoils of Marathon, and a nearby base carries a Marathon inscription. Why is the honest verdict only "possibly"?

options.A: Many archaeologists date the building's style a few years before 490 BCE, and the inscription belongs to the terrace, which may have held a separate monument
options.B: The treasury was built by Sparta, not Athens, and only later taken over
options.C: The treasury is a 1906 replica with no original blocks, so it cannot be dated
options.D: Pausanias never visited Delphi and invented the story from a distance

questions.explanation: The inscription saying the Athenians dedicated the spoils of Marathon sounds conclusive, but it stands on a triangular terrace beside the treasury, which may have held a separate monument. Many archaeologists date the building's style to around 500 BCE, before Marathon. So Athens certainly used the spot to advertise Marathon, but whether the victory paid for the building is unsettled. The French rebuilt it in 1903–1906 from its original blocks, which rules out option C.

questions.chapter: Day 12: Delphi
questions.question_text: On the polygonal wall you read a record in which a woman is "sold" to Pythian Apollo, with a clause that she must stay and serve her former owner until the owner's death. What does that clause mean?

options.A: The sale is fake, and she remains enslaved forever
options.B: Apollo's priests now own her and will put her to work in the temple
options.C: Her freedom is recorded and guaranteed, but under *paramone* it becomes complete only after years of further service
options.D: She must pay the price again each year to keep her freedom

questions.explanation: In a Delphic manumission, the owner "sold" the enslaved person to Apollo, but the money was the person's own savings, and since no one could claim a god's property, the person became free. The record named the archon, a guarantor, and witnesses. Many records add *paramone*, "remaining": the freed person had to stay and serve, often until the owner's death, before freedom was complete. The god did not keep her as a servant (option B); the sale was the legal route to freedom.

questions.chapter: Day 12: Delphi
questions.question_text: The bronze Serpent Column stands in Istanbul's Hippodrome, while Delphi keeps its base and a bronze copy. Why does the chapter say neither city tells the story alone?

options.A: Istanbul has the object, Delphi has the place where it stood beside the altar, and the written sources supply the rest
options.B: Both columns are modern copies, so the story survives only in books
options.C: The column was cut in half, and each city holds one piece of the bronze
options.D: Istanbul's column is a different monument with no link to Delphi

questions.explanation: The Serpent Column was cast after Plataea in 479 BCE to hold a golden tripod beside Apollo's altar, and Constantine moved it to his capital by 330 CE. Istanbul has the twisted bronze trunk and the upper jaw of one head; Delphi has the base near the altar and a bronze copy showing how tall it rose. Herodotus gives the spoils and place, Thucydides the erased boast, and Pausanias the loss of the gold in the Third Sacred War. Istanbul's bronze is the original (option B).

questions.chapter: Day 12: Delphi
questions.question_text: Which description fits the Pythian Games after their reorganization in 582 BCE?

options.A: A purely athletic festival held every year, with prizes of gold coins
options.B: A festival every four years that put music first, then athletics and horse races, with a laurel crown as the prize
options.C: A chariot race held only for the rulers of Sicily
options.D: A festival of drama in which playwrights competed with tragedies

questions.explanation: The Pythian Games began as a contest in singing a hymn to Apollo with the *kithara*. After the First Sacred War, the Amphictyonic League reorganized them in 582 BCE as a festival every four years, adding athletics and horse races. Music came first in the program, then events in the stadium, then the chariot and horse races on the plain. The prize was a crown of laurel, Apollo's tree. Sicilian rulers did compete in the chariot races, but the games were open to Greeks from every city.

questions.chapter: Day 12: Delphi
questions.question_text: At the round Tholos in the Athena Pronaia sanctuary, a guide says with confidence that it was a shrine to an earth goddess. How should you weigh that?

options.A: Accept it, because Vitruvius records the building's purpose in detail
options.B: Accept it, because all round buildings in Greece were shrines to earth goddesses
options.C: Treat it as one proposal among several, since no ancient writer says what the Tholos was for
options.D: Reject it, because the Tholos is known to have been the oracle's treasury

questions.explanation: The Tholos, of the early 4th century BCE, had 20 Doric columns outside and 10 Corinthian columns inside. Vitruvius says its architect, Theodorus of Phocaea, wrote a book about it, but no ancient writer says what it was for, so option A is wrong. Scholars have proposed a shrine to an earth goddess, a hero's memorial, a hall for a lost rite, or a treasury. The best-preserved building can still be the least explained, and option D claims a certainty no one has.

questions.chapter: Day 12: Delphi
questions.question_text: Why did the bronze Charioteer of Delphi survive when thousands of other bronzes at the sanctuary did not?

options.A: It was carried to Rome by Nero and returned in the 19th century
options.B: It was kept inside the Temple of Apollo, where looters never entered
options.C: It was made of a special alloy that could not be melted down
options.D: It was buried and forgotten, probably by the earthquake of 373 BCE, until French excavators found it in 1896

questions.explanation: The Charioteer, made around 478 to 470 BCE for a Pythian chariot victory, was found in 1896 buried near the temple, probably by the earthquake of 373 BCE. Thousands of bronzes once stood at Delphi; Nero alone took about 500, and most of the rest were melted for their metal. This one survived because it was lost, so the museum shows what escaped, not a fair sample. Nero's bronzes went to Rome and did not come back (option A).

questions.chapter: Day 12: Delphi
questions.question_text: What trade-off does the chapter name in the French excavation of Delphi that began in 1892?

options.A: The excavators destroyed the temple's foundations to reach older layers
options.B: The village of Kastri, which stood on the sanctuary, was bought, demolished, and moved so the ruins could be uncovered
options.C: Greece gave France the Charioteer and the Delphic Hymns in exchange for the right to dig
options.D: The excavators rebuilt the whole sanctuary in concrete, hiding the original stones

questions.explanation: By the time western travelers came, the ruins lay under the mountain village of Kastri, whose houses stood on the terraces and reused ancient stones. After years of negotiation, Greece gave the excavation rights to the French School at Athens; Kastri's houses were bought and demolished, and its people moved to a new village that took the name Delphi. For them it meant losing homes, fields, and family graves. The sanctuary we walk exists because a village was taken away. The Charioteer is in the Delphi museum (option C).

questions.chapter: Day 12: Delphi
questions.question_text: What lesson about students' learning records does the chapter draw from the freedom records on the polygonal wall?

options.A: A record is trusted when a neutral keeper stands behind it and the person it describes can always point to it, so learning records should be portable and under the learner's control
options.B: Records should be carved in stone so that no one can ever correct them
options.C: Learning records are best kept private inside each school's own system
options.D: Students should not have records of their achievements, since records were once used to control people

questions.explanation: At Delphi, freedom was written in stone in the busiest place in the sanctuary, dated, witnessed, and backed by a guarantor and the god, so a woman whose freedom was questioned could point to the wall. Today a student's learning leaves records in many systems that belong to the system, not the learner, and they disappear or stay locked when the student moves on. Option C describes exactly that problem. The chapter's lesson is a trusted keeper plus records the learner controls.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
questions.question_text: Amazon's experimental hiring program was edited to ignore words like "women's," yet the project was dropped. Why does removing a column such as gender not remove the bias?

options.A: The engineers forgot to delete the gender column from the training data
options.B: Hiring algorithms are deliberately programmed to prefer men
options.C: Other details, such as a club, a college, a first name, or an address, can act as proxies that carry the same information
options.D: The model was trained on too few résumés to learn anything useful

questions.explanation: The program was trained on about ten years of résumés, most from men, and learned to mark down résumés mentioning "women's" or two women's colleges. Engineers removed those terms but could not be sure the model would not find other ways to sort candidates. Details like a club, college, first name, or home address can act as proxies, stand-ins carrying the same information. The bias was learned from past decisions, not deliberately programmed (option B). Well-run systems are tested for unequal results across groups.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
questions.question_text: A restaurant app trained on 50,000 Athens reviews, 90 percent written by visitors staying near their hotels, keeps recommending places near the Plaka. What is the best way to correct for its bias?

options.A: Trust it more, because 50,000 reviews is a very large sample
options.B: Ask whose experience was in the data, and add a voice it left out, such as someone who lives here
options.C: Choose the lowest-rated restaurant, since the ratings must be reversed
options.D: Use a different app trained on the same reviews with a newer design

questions.explanation: The model is accurate about its data and biased about the city: it rarely recommends a neighborhood taverna, not because the food is worse but because few reviewers went there. Millions of examples from the same kind of person still leave everyone else out, and nothing in the numbers warns you, so option A is the trap the chapter names. The fix is to ask whose experience was in the data and whether yours is like theirs, then add a missing voice, such as a local.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
questions.question_text: A language model completing "On Sundays the Grand Bazaar is ___" gives *closed* a 45 percent probability and *open* 30 percent. At temperature 1, about how often will it answer "open"?

options.A: Never, because the model always picks the most likely word
options.B: About 7 times in 10, because higher temperature favors unlikely words
options.C: Exactly half the time, because there are two main choices
options.D: About 3 times in 10, because at temperature 1 it samples in proportion to the probabilities

questions.explanation: At temperature 1, a model picks each next word at random in proportion to its probability, so a word with 30 percent is chosen about 3 times in 10. Option A describes temperature 0, which always takes the single most likely word. The model has not changed its mind about the facts; it samples from what is likely to be written, and likely is not the same as true. That is why the same question can get different answers on different days.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
questions.question_text: According to the chapter, what three things does a meaningful "human in the loop" need?

options.A: Time to think, information the machine lacks, and freedom to overrule it without penalty
options.B: A faster computer, a larger dataset, and a second machine to check the first
options.C: A signature on every decision, a manager's approval, and a written log
options.D: Training in programming, access to the code, and a vote on the model's design

questions.explanation: A human in the loop reviews and is responsible for the decisions an automated system recommends. But people tend to accept a machine's recommendation even when they have reason to doubt it, a tendency called automation bias. A loan officer who approves whatever the score says is in the loop on paper only. A meaningful loop needs time to think, information the machine lacks, and freedom to overrule without penalty. The Athenian Assembly arguing over the wooden-wall answer was a human in the loop of the oracle.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
questions.question_text: A school's early-warning system labels a student "high risk," and she is moved to a less demanding class. How could this prediction feed itself?

options.A: It cannot, because a prediction has no effect on the outcome it predicts
options.B: Lower expectations and an easier class mean she learns less, which raises her risk score and confirms the label
options.C: The label alerts tutors, who raise her grades and prove the model wrong
options.D: The model deletes her record once she is moved, so no further prediction is made

questions.explanation: A self-fulfilling prophecy comes true because it was made. If a "high-risk" label leads to lower expectations or a less demanding class, the student may learn less, which raises her risk score, which confirms the label. Research beginning with *Pygmalion in the Classroom* suggests expectations can affect results, though how strongly is debated. The chapter's test is what the school does with the flag: one that brings a tutor helps (as in option C), while one that lowers the challenge harms.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
questions.question_text: A forecaster said "90 percent chance of rain" on ten days, and it rained on 6 of them. How should you describe this forecaster?

options.A: Well calibrated, because it rained on most of the days
options.B: Underconfident, because the forecaster should have said 100 percent
options.C: Overconfident, because forecasts of 90 percent came true only 60 percent of the time
options.D: Perfect, because a percentage forecast can never be proven wrong

questions.explanation: Calibration measures whether a forecaster's probabilities match how often things happen. Saying 90 percent when the true frequency is 60 percent is overconfident; the chapter's Forecaster A, who said 70 percent and got rain on 7 of 10 days, was well calibrated. On the Brier score, B's confident forecasts are punished heavily on the dry days and score worse than saying "50 percent" every day. A single day cannot prove a percentage wrong, but many days together can (option D).

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
questions.question_text: Two sources offer predictions. One is famous for a dramatic correct call that was written down after the event. The other has a public record of many dated forecasts, misses included, scored by someone else. Which deserves more trust, and why?

options.A: The public, scored record, because trust should rest on many predictions recorded before the outcomes
options.B: The dramatic call, because one spectacular hit shows special insight
options.C: Both equally, because any source can be right by chance
options.D: Neither, because no prediction about the future can ever be checked

questions.explanation: Track record and trust holds that a source deserves trust in proportion to its record of predictions written down before the outcomes. Delphi's 1,140 years of trust rested on stories of hits recorded after they "came true," with the misses forgotten, the weakness of option B. The track records worth trusting are public, cover many predictions, include the misses, and are scored by someone other than the forecaster. Testable, dated claims make checking possible, which rules out option D.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
questions.question_text: The chapter compares Delphi as a "data hub" with a large language model. What warning applies to both?

options.A: Both forget everything they hear after a short time
options.B: Both were designed to keep information secret from ordinary people
options.C: Both speak only in riddles that no one can interpret
options.D: Both gather many voices unevenly: those who could afford the trip, or who write a great deal online

questions.explanation: Envoys reached Delphi from Sicily to the Black Sea, bringing news with their questions, and some historians suggest that flow of information helps explain the oracle's sensible practical answers, though no archive proves it. A language model is a hub too, compressing an enormous number of voices. But Delphi's envoys came mostly from cities that could afford the journey, and a model's text comes mostly from people and languages that write a great deal online. A hub knows much less about people who never make the trip.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
questions.question_text: How does the chapter describe the reversal between Delphi and modern prediction when it comes to consent?

options.A: At Delphi predictions were forced on everyone, while today we choose every prediction made about us
options.B: At Delphi and today alike, people must pay before any prediction is made about them
options.C: At Delphi every prediction was asked for, while today systems predict about us without our asking, from data we may not know we gave
options.D: At Delphi only kings were predicted about, while today only governments make predictions

questions.explanation: At Delphi, a consultant climbed the mountain, paid the fee, and put a question; no one received an oracle about themselves without asking. Today the arrangement is reversed: on a single Sunday, a fraud model checked our lunch purchase in Arachova and a phone keyboard predicted our next word, all without our asking. The chapter counts scale and consent among the limits of the oracle parallel, making the modern situation harder than the ancient one. Option A reverses the two eras.

questions.chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
questions.question_text: A chart shows an AI measure doubling every five months, and a headline extends it ten years into the future. Which analysis fits the chapter's warning?

options.A: The projection is guaranteed, because doubling curves always continue
options.B: The projection is worthless, because no trend in AI has ever been measured
options.C: Doubling is too slow to matter, since the measure barely changes in a year
options.D: Such a curve grows about fivefold a year, but it assumes the forces behind it continue, and many such curves level off into an S-shape at a limit

questions.explanation: Something that doubles every five months grows about fivefold in a year and nearly 150-fold in three years, so option C is wrong. But the forecast assumes the forces behind the trend continue, and many curves that looked like endless doubling were the early part of an S-shape that leveled off at a limit such as energy, money, or data. A small change in the doubling time also changes the long-range answer enormously. AI doubling curves are measured trends with wide uncertainty, not promises.

questions.chapter: Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today
questions.question_text: What was the Antikythera mechanism?

options.A: A Roman water clock used to time speeches in the law courts
options.B: A bronze statue of a youth recovered from a shipwreck off Crete
options.C: A Byzantine astrolabe used by sailors to find their position at sea
options.D: A hand-cranked device of bronze gears from the 2nd century BCE that modeled the cycles of the Sun and Moon

questions.explanation: Sponge divers found a Roman-era shipwreck off Antikythera in 1900; it had sunk about 70–60 BCE. Among the finds was a lump of corroded bronze and wood, and in 1902 Valerios Stais saw a gear wheel in it. The surviving 82 fragments hold at least 30 gears from a shoebox-sized box with dials and a crank, covered in tiny Greek inscriptions. Turning the crank modeled the Sun, the Moon, and probably the planets. Option B describes the Antikythera Youth, a statue from the same wreck.

questions.chapter: Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today
questions.question_text: The chapter says the Antikythera mechanism "sits between the tripod and the algorithm." Which analysis explains that position?

options.A: Like the oracle, it gave different answers to rich and poor; like a modern model, it learned from new examples
options.B: Unlike the oracle, its answers were the same for all, fixed in advance, and open to inspection; unlike a learning model, its rules never changed
options.C: It was a religious object consulted at Delphi, and also the first computer to learn from data
options.D: It combined the Pythia's trance with a written record of every answer she gave

questions.explanation: Compared with the oracle of Chapter 17, the mechanism gave the same answer to anyone who turned the crank, its answer was fixed before the event so it could be checked, and its model could be inspected gear by gear. Compared with the models of Chapter 19, it lacked one thing: its rules were set once by its maker from centuries of records and never changed, so a wrong ratio stayed wrong. A machine-learning model adjusts its own rules from examples, which rules out options A and C.

questions.chapter: Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today
questions.question_text: A Greek parapegma, a stone peg calendar, lists the yearly risings of the stars and the weather expected with them. Which of its predictions should you trust more, and why?

options.A: The star risings, because they repeat exactly every year, while the weather does not
options.B: The weather forecasts, because they were based on centuries of farmers' experience
options.C: Both equally, because both were carved in stone by the same astronomers
options.D: Neither, because ancient calendars could not predict anything

questions.explanation: Babylonian astronomers found that eclipses and the positions of the Moon and planets repeat in regular cycles, so once a cycle is known, prediction becomes counting. Star risings repeat exactly every year, so a fixed model could predict them for centuries; the weather does not repeat, so the forecasts tied to the stars were far less reliable. Being carved by the same hand (option C) does not make them equally reliable. The chapter's test: before trusting any prediction machine, ask whether the thing it predicts actually repeats.

questions.chapter: Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today
questions.question_text: The Temple of Olympian Zeus was begun about 520 BCE and finished by Hadrian about 650 years later. How did Aristotle use the unfinished temple in his *Politics*?

options.A: As proof that democracy builds greater temples than tyranny
options.B: As a model of the perfect Corinthian proportions for future architects
options.C: As an example of tyrants keeping their subjects busy and poor with vast building projects
options.D: As evidence that Zeus had abandoned Athens for Olympia

questions.explanation: The temple was begun by the tyrant family of the Peisistratids and finished by Hadrian in 131–132 CE, with 104 Corinthian columns about 17 m tall, of which 15 still stand. In his *Politics*, Aristotle argued that tyrants keep their subjects busy and poor with vast building projects, and he named the Peisistratids' temple beside the pyramids of Egypt. Its long building history reads like a summary of Athens's masters, including Antiochus IV and Sulla.

questions.chapter: Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today
questions.question_text: What was the Athens Polytechnic uprising, remembered every November 17?

options.A: A riot against Ottoman rule that began the Greek War of Independence
options.B: A student occupation in November 1973 against the military junta, crushed when a tank broke through the gate
options.C: A protest against austerity during the debt crisis of 2010
options.D: A strike by university teachers demanding higher wages in 1981

questions.explanation: From November 14 to 17, 1973, students occupied the National Technical University on Patission Street to protest the colonels' junta, which had ruled since April 21, 1967. They broadcast from a makeshift radio station, and thousands joined them. Early on November 17 a tank crashed through the main gate; research documents at least 24 civilians killed. The junta fell in July 1974. The bent gate is preserved as a memorial, and a march sets out each year on November 17.

questions.chapter: Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today
questions.question_text: During the debt crisis, Greece's economy shrank by about a quarter. If it stood at 100 before the crisis, how much must it grow to return to 100?

options.A: About 25 percent, the same as the loss
options.B: About 15 percent, since growth compounds each year
options.C: About 50 percent, since debt doubles the loss
options.D: About one third, because growth is measured from the new, lower base of 75

questions.explanation: A fall of about a quarter leaves 75. To climb back to 100, the economy must grow by 25 ÷ 75, or one third, not one quarter (option A), because growth is measured from the new, lower base. At a steady 2 percent a year the climb takes about 15 years, and at 1 percent about 29 years. Option B confuses the number of years with the percentage needed. That is why a crisis that "ended" in 2018 still shapes wages and drove many young Greeks abroad.

questions.chapter: Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today
questions.question_text: Greek coffee is made exactly like the Turkish coffee of Istanbul. Why do Greeks call it by a different name?

options.A: The European Union required a Greek name when Greece adopted the euro
options.B: Greek coffee uses a different bean grown on Crete
options.C: After the Turkish military intervention in Cyprus in 1974, "Turkish coffee" came to feel wrong, and the name changed
options.D: Greeks invented the drink first, and Turks later borrowed it

questions.explanation: Greek coffee is ground fine, boiled in a long-handled *briki*, and poured unfiltered, the same drink as Turkish coffee. Until the 1970s Greeks usually called it "Turkish coffee" too. After the Turkish military intervention in Cyprus in 1974, the name came to feel wrong to many Greeks, and within a few years "Greek coffee" was the usual name. The coffee did not change; the word did, because a word can carry a wound. Coffee reached Istanbul from Yemen, so option D has no support.

questions.chapter: Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today
questions.question_text: A 2020 review of randomized school tutoring trials found an average effect of about 0.37 standard deviations. Where does that move the average tutored student, compared with a class that was not tutored?

options.A: From the 50th to about the 64th percentile
options.B: From the 50th to about the 98th percentile
options.C: From a score of 50 percent to a score of 87 percent on the test
options.D: Nowhere meaningful, since effects below one standard deviation are too small to matter

questions.explanation: An effect size states the difference between groups in standard deviations, and the useful translation is a percentile. About a third of a standard deviation moves the average student from the 50th to about the 64th percentile, a real gain. Option B is Bloom's famous 2 sigma result, which came from small, short studies and has not held up at full size. A percentile is not a test score (option C), and the chapter calls even smaller effects large by education research standards (option D).

questions.chapter: Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today
questions.question_text: How does mastery learning differ from conventional teaching?

options.A: It holds time fixed and lets mastery vary, so grades spread out across the class
options.B: It lets the fastest students skip every test and move on at once
options.C: It replaces teachers entirely with self-paced software
options.D: It holds mastery fixed and lets time vary, giving targeted practice and a second check to students below the threshold

questions.explanation: Conventional teaching holds time fixed: everyone gets three weeks on fractions, and the grades spread out, which is option A. Mastery learning, proposed by Bloom in 1968, holds mastery fixed and lets time vary. A student who scores 70 percent on the fractions check does not move on with a C; she gets targeted practice on what she missed, takes a second check, and moves on when she reaches a threshold such as 80 or 90 percent. It appears in both of Bloom's stronger conditions.

questions.chapter: Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today
questions.question_text: Socrates' warning that writing weakens memory survives only because Plato wrote it down, and similar fears returned with printing and calculators. What does this pattern suggest about worries over AI?

options.A: The worries are always wrong, so concerns about AI over-reliance can be ignored
options.B: The fear recurs with every new learning tool; it is worth taking seriously, but the answer lies in how the tool is used, not in refusing it
options.C: Each new tool has made people steadily less intelligent, so AI should be banned from schools
options.D: Only writing was ever feared, so the comparison with AI is mistaken

questions.explanation: In the *Phaedrus*, King Thamus warns that writing is "an aid not to memory, but to reminiscence," yet we know the warning only through Plato's careful writing. The abbot Trithemius urged monks to keep copying by hand, and had his praise of scribes printed; teachers later argued over calculators. The fear recurs, but the chapter also says AI over-reliance is real, so option A goes too far. Guardrails decide whether a tutor helps or harms, which rules out a blanket ban.

questions.chapter: Going Home: Learning With Communities, Not To Them
questions.question_text: What has UNESCO long said about the language children should learn in?

options.A: Every child should learn first in a major world language, such as English, to reach the most knowledge
options.B: The best medium for teaching is the mother tongue of the pupil, and many people lack education in a language they understand
options.C: Children should learn two foreign languages before learning to read their own
options.D: Mother-tongue schooling works well even without trained teachers or books in that language

questions.explanation: A 1953 UNESCO report called it axiomatic that "the best medium for teaching is the mother tongue of the pupil." A 2016 UNESCO policy paper asked, "If you don't understand, how can you learn?", and estimated that as much as 40 percent of the world's people lack education in a language they speak or understand. Research finds that a strong first-language start supports a second language. But mother-tongue programs succeed only with trained teachers and books in that language, which rules out option D.

questions.chapter: Going Home: Learning With Communities, Not To Them
questions.question_text: Istanbul printed its first Ottoman book in Arabic script about 275 years after Gutenberg. What lesson does the chapter draw about the cost of delaying a technology?

options.A: Every new learning technology should be adopted at once, since delay is always the greater harm
options.B: The delay was caused by ignorance, since no one in Istanbul knew how printing worked
options.C: Delay costs nothing, because manuscripts served readers just as well as print
options.D: Count what waiting costs and who pays it, while remembering that printing made copies, not readers, and that rushing has costs too

questions.explanation: The cost of delaying technology is real: books not printed and readers not made. But Istanbul had Jewish, Armenian, and Greek presses long before 1729, so the delay was not ignorance (option B). Even after the press came, most people could not read the script, so printing made copies, not readers. And waiting has an opposite cost: a school can buy AI faster than it can judge it. The lesson is not "adopt everything at once" but "count what waiting costs, and who pays it."

questions.chapter: Going Home: Learning With Communities, Not To Them
questions.question_text: A school district plans to bring AI tutors into every classroom. Applying the lesson of scribal resistance, whom should the planners make sure to hear first?

options.A: Only the technology vendors, since they understand the tools best
options.B: Only the parents of the highest-achieving students, since they will benefit most
options.C: The teachers, aides, tutoring companies, and publishers whose skill or living depends on the way things are done now
options.D: No one in particular, since resistance to change is always irrational

questions.explanation: Scribal resistance is opposition from people whose skill, income, or prestige depended on an old technology: Homer's reciters, Demetrius the silversmith, Ottoman copyists, and the abbot Trithemius. They were not irrational: Demetrius was right about his market, and the copyists were right that the press would end their way of life, which rules out option D. Resistance is information about who stands to lose. The scribes' successors today, teachers, aides, tutoring companies, and publishers, are owed a hearing.

questions.chapter: Going Home: Learning With Communities, Not To Them
questions.question_text: Drawing up a ledger for the 1928 alphabet reform, the chapter sorts its costs into those that came with any change of script and those that came from the method. Which costs belong to the method?

options.A: The ban on the old script, the absence of a vote, and the speed set by a one-party state
options.B: Children no longer learning the old letters once schools taught the new ones
options.C: The new alphabet's one letter for each sound, which made reading easier to learn
options.D: The rise in literacy, which happened only because the reform was imposed quickly

questions.explanation: Some costs come with any change of script: once schools teach new letters, children stop learning the old ones unless someone teaches both, which is option B. Others came from choices of method: the ban on the old script, the absence of a vote, and the speed set by a one-party state. Those choices are why the reform is still argued over. The ledger does not say whether the reform was right; it shows that speed bought by command is paid for later, often by the grandchildren.

questions.chapter: Going Home: Learning With Communities, Not To Them
questions.question_text: Which three questions make up the chapter's test for evangelism's shadow?

options.A: How much does it cost? How fast can it spread? How many will adopt it?
options.B: Is the news true? Is it new? Is it popular?
options.C: Who paid for it? Who built it? Who will maintain it?
options.D: Who chose? What is treated as the obstacle? What happens to those who say no?

questions.explanation: Evangelism's shadow is the harm that follows when good news is imposed rather than chosen, or when its carriers treat those who decline it with contempt. Three questions would have caught each shadow on the route. Who chose? The 1928 alphabet was chosen for Turks, not by them. What is treated as the obstacle? Residential schools treated a child's language as the obstacle. What happens to those who say no? Paul's later readers turned his words against those who declined the message.

questions.chapter: Going Home: Learning With Communities, Not To Them
questions.question_text: An AI reading program for a rural region requires that all lessons be in the national language and asks teachers to discourage children from using their home language in class. Which part of the shadow test does it fail most clearly?

options.A: "Who chose?", because the program is free of charge
options.B: "What is treated as the obstacle?", because it treats the children's own language as something to get around
options.C: "What happens to those who say no?", because families can always opt out
options.D: It passes all three tests, because the program teaches reading

questions.explanation: The plan treats the children's home language as the obstacle to learning, the same mistake as the church-run residential schools in Canada, where the Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported that many Indigenous children were punished for speaking their own languages. The intention was to bring education; the method taught children that their language, and so their families, stood in the way. A free program can still fail "Who chose?", and nothing in the plan shows families can opt out, so option C assumes too much.

questions.chapter: Going Home: Learning With Communities, Not To Them
questions.question_text: A ministry plans to machine-translate a reading series into a small regional language and send it straight to classrooms. What is the main flaw in the plan, and what is the remedy?

options.A: AI translates small languages poorly but fluently, so fluent speakers from the community must check samples and fix errors before children see them
options.B: AI translation is too expensive for small languages, so the series should stay in the national language
options.C: Machine translation is always word-for-word, so it should only be used for science lessons
options.D: There is no flaw, because a smooth-sounding translation is a correct translation

questions.explanation: AI translation could put lessons into small languages for a tiny fraction of human translation costs, so option B is wrong. But AI systems learn from digitized text, mostly in a few large languages, so they translate smaller languages poorly, often fluently and wrongly; fluent is not the same as right (option D). The remedy is to involve the speakers, as Masakhane, "we build together," does for African languages, and to have a fluent speaker review a sample before any lesson reaches a child.

questions.chapter: Going Home: Learning With Communities, Not To Them
questions.question_text: The chapter says "the last step is decided at the second." What does it mean?

options.A: The second year of any reform decides whether it will last
options.B: A change should be tested twice before it is announced
options.C: Those left out at the end are usually those absent when the opening was designed, so inviting them in early shrinks who is left out
options.D: Resistance always comes second, so leaders should ignore early objections

questions.explanation: Chapter 2's four-step pattern runs: learning locked up, opened by a new technology or institution, resisted, and widened but never all the way. The people left out at the fourth step are most often the people who were not in the room when the opening, the second step, was designed. Inviting them in at step two is the cheapest way to shrink step four. That is the core of education with communities: designing, running, and judging a change with the people it serves.

questions.chapter: Going Home: Learning With Communities, Not To Them
questions.question_text: Which example from the route is the strongest case of education done *with* a community rather than *to* it?

options.A: Justinian's law of 529 deciding by belief who could teach philosophy
options.B: Turkey's Village Institutes, which trained teachers from village families and sent them home to teach
options.C: The Roman Senate's expulsion of Greek philosophers and teachers of rhetoric in 161 BCE
options.D: The 1923 population exchange, which sorted millions by religion without asking their language

questions.explanation: Education with communities designs, runs, and judges a change together with the people it serves, in their language and with their hands on how it continues. The Village Institutes trained teachers from village families and sent them home, a piece of the 1928 era built closer to communities. The other options are top-down decisions made far away: Justinian's law, the Senate's expulsion, and the exchange convention that decided where millions would live without asking what language they spoke at home.

questions.chapter: Going Home: Learning With Communities, Not To Them
questions.question_text: You are writing a good news message about AI and education from your visit to Rhodes. Which draft best meets the chapter's four tests?

options.A: "AI will transform every school in the world, and anyone who resists is standing in the way of progress."
options.B: "I read online that Rhodes once had famous teachers, and AI can now replace teachers everywhere."
options.C: "AI tutors are cheap and fast, so governments should install them in every classroom this year."
options.D: "In Rhodes's Old Town we heard how a list of names helped find every Jewish family in 1944. An AI tutor that knows each child could help, but only if her family and teachers decide what data it keeps."

questions.explanation: A good news message comes from a story we actually saw, is honest about the cost, names who the good news is with, and is heard as good by the people it concerns. Draft D starts from what we learned on Rhodes, names the risk of learner data, and puts the family and teachers in charge. Option A despises those who decline, the shadow's mark. Option B is not a story we saw, and option C is speed by command, with no one asked.
